projectTitle: Caldera Energy Co-op: Trustworthy Billing From Real-Time Telemetry, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a serverless AWS data platform — Kinesis, Lambda, Glue, and Redshift, for one fictional solar co-op, from a manual billing spreadsheet to automated, auditable net-metering credits.
businessContext:
**Caldera Energy Co-op** is a fictional regional renewable-energy cooperative: roughly 5,000 residential and small-business solar installations, each with a smart inverter reporting performance telemetry every few minutes. For years, the co-op's billing team produced monthly net-metering credit totals through a manual CSV export and spreadsheet process — slow, error-prone, and the cause of a real member billing dispute after a copy-paste error duplicated a week of data. Meanwhile, the field operations team has no timely visibility into underperforming installations that need a maintenance visit.

You've been brought in as an AWS Data Engineer to replace that manual process with a real, automated, serverless data platform: real-time ingestion from the inverter fleet, a proper data lake, and trustworthy billing numbers. This series follows that build end to end — including a real production incident where Kinesis's at-least-once delivery semantics briefly double-counted a batch of readings, caught and fixed before it ever reached a member's bill.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Caldera Energy Co-op has: inverter telemetry streaming through Amazon Kinesis (`caldera-inverter-telemetry`) and an AWS Lambda function (`ingest-inverter-events`) into a raw S3 data lake (`caldera-lake-raw`); an AWS Glue Crawler and ETL job cataloging and cleaning that data into a curated S3 location (`caldera-lake-curated`, catalog `caldera_energy`); two governed Amazon Redshift Gold tables (`gold.installation_performance_gold` for daily per-installation performance, `gold.monthly_billing_gold` for monthly net-metering credits); a Step Functions state machine orchestrating the nightly pipeline; Terraform-provisioned infrastructure with CI-tested Glue scripts and Terraform plans; CloudWatch/SNS monitoring; and a real Kinesis-retry double-counting bug found, root-caused, fixed, and backfilled before it ever reached a member's bill. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Kinesis, Lambda, Glue, and Redshift fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Caldera Energy: Why Billing Can't Trust the Monthly Generation Numbers
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: a member's net-metering credit tripled with no clear explanation, exposing that Caldera Energy Co-op's manual, spreadsheet-driven billing process has no way to validate itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build one complete serverless data platform for a fictional regional renewable-energy cooperative, **Caldera Energy Co-op** — roughly 5,000 residential and small-business solar installations, each with a smart inverter streaming performance telemetry (kWh generated, panel health status) every few minutes, and two teams who currently have almost no reliable way to use any of it. The field operations team can't tell which installations need a maintenance truck roll until a member calls weeks after their system starts degrading. The billing and finance team closes out monthly net-metering credits with a manual CSV export and a spreadsheet process — one that just produced a number nobody on the team could fully explain to a worried member.

By the end of this series you'll have inverter telemetry streaming into an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, an AWS Lambda function landing raw events into an S3 data lake, an AWS Glue Data Catalog and PySpark ETL job cleaning and curating that data, and two governed Gold-layer tables in Amazon Redshift — one for daily installation performance, one for monthly billing — that both Caldera teams can finally trust. This video starts where every real AWS Data Engineer project starts: not with a Kinesis stream, but with a room full of people trying to explain why their numbers don't add up.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a lemonade stand with 5,000 different lemonade machines spread across town, and each machine sends a little text message every few minutes saying how much lemonade it just made. Right now, almost nobody reads those texts — the only way anyone finds out a machine is broken is if the machine's owner calls to complain, weeks after it stopped working right. And at the end of the month, someone has to add up every single text by hand in a notebook to figure out how much to pay each machine owner. That's slow, and sometimes the notebook math is wrong.

That's exactly Caldera Energy Co-op's problem, except the lemonade machines are solar panels and the notebook is a spreadsheet. One panel owner, Harlan Voss, just called because his monthly payment tripled for no reason he could see — and the billing team couldn't fully explain why either, because their process has no way to double-check itself. Your job is to build a real computer system that watches all 5,000 machines as the texts come in and does the monthly math automatically and correctly, every single time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a data engineering engagement, and like most real ones, the trigger wasn't a strategic initiative — it was a complaint. Caldera's VP of Member Services, Renata Vance, called this meeting after a member, Harlan Voss (installation INV-04821, in the co-op's Willow Creek service area), phoned in alarmed that his net-metering credit had jumped from a typical ~$84 a month to $211.60, with no corresponding change in weather, panel condition, or system size. Billing & Finance Manager Priya Shah eventually traced it to a copy-paste error in the monthly rollup workbook — one week of that installation's generation data had been pasted into the sheet twice — but she only found it because Harlan called. Nothing in the current process would have caught it on its own.

That's the real finding to leave this meeting with: the problem isn't one bad spreadsheet formula, it's that Caldera's billing pipeline has zero built-in validation and depends entirely on members noticing their own bill looks wrong. Separately, Field Operations Manager Desmond Okafor raises a second, related gap: his team currently learns about an underperforming installation — a failing inverter, a cracked panel, a shading issue — only when a member calls about a disappointing bill, often weeks after the fault started, during which time that installation has quietly been losing the member money and the co-op credibility. Both problems trace back to the same root cause: telemetry exists, every few minutes, from every installation, and nobody is using any of it in anything close to real time.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Walk in already knowing what you don't know

A vague ask like "fix our billing numbers" hides a list of real ambiguities. Before the meeting, write them down:

- Is the problem the billing calculation itself, or the manual process that produces it?
- How is "generation" currently measured — gross kWh reported by the inverter, or something adjusted along the way?
- Is there any automated check on the monthly numbers today, or is a member complaint the only error-detection mechanism Caldera has?
- Is the maintenance-visibility problem the same root cause as the billing problem, or a separate one that just happens to look similar?
- What's the actual scale here — how much telemetry is 5,000 installations reporting every few minutes really producing?

## Step 2 — Interview each stakeholder, and let them disagree about what matters most

Renata Vance, Caldera's VP of Member Services, opens the meeting:

```
RENATA: We had a member call last week -- Harlan Voss, out in Willow
        Creek -- whose net-metering credit jumped from around $84 to
        $211.60 in one month. He wasn't even angry, he was worried we'd
        made a mistake in his favor and would claw it back later.
        Priya's team spent two days figuring out why, and the honest
        answer is we got lucky he called. I don't want "lucky" to be
        our quality control.
```

Priya Shah, Billing & Finance Manager, fills in what she found:

```
PRIYA: It was a copy-paste error in the monthly rollup workbook -- one
       week of Harlan's installation data got pasted into the sheet
       twice. Nothing flagged it. Nothing CAN flag it, the way we
       build that workbook today -- it's a manual CSV export from our
       monitoring portal into a spreadsheet, every month, for all
       5,000 installations. I believe this month's numbers. I can't
       prove last month's were right, and I can't promise next
       month's will be either.
```

Desmond Okafor, Field Operations Manager, raises the second half of the problem:

```
DESMOND: My team's version of this is worse, honestly -- we don't even
         have a wrong number, we have no number. Every inverter
         reports its health every few minutes. We don't look at any
         of it until a member calls about a bill that looks low, and
         by then whatever broke has probably been broken for weeks. I
         need to know an installation is failing the same day it
         starts failing, not the day someone notices their bill.
```

## Step 3 — Size the actual problem before assuming the fix

Ask the follow-up that turns feelings into numbers:

```
YOU: Renata, how many installations are we talking about total, and
     how often do they report?
RENATA: About 5,000 across our service territory. Each inverter phones
        home every few minutes -- kWh generated, a panel health
        status.
YOU: So that's over a million telemetry events a day, every day, that
     nobody is systematically looking at until billing close -- or
     until a complaint.
RENATA: ...I hadn't put it that way, but yes.
```

That reframing — from "one bad spreadsheet number" to "a million-plus untouched events a day" — is the moment this stops being a billing-fix conversation and becomes a data platform conversation.

## Step 4 — Separate the two real problems, and don't let either one eat the other

```
PROBLEM 1 (billing trust): The monthly net-metering credit process is
manual, unvalidated, and only caught its last known error because the
affected member happened to call. Harlan Voss's case (INV-04821,
$84 -> $211.60, traced to a duplicated week of data in the rollup
workbook) is the forcing event, not the whole problem.

PROBLEM 2 (maintenance visibility): Underperforming or failed
installations are invisible to Field Operations until a member
complains, by which time the installation has likely been degraded
for weeks -- costing billing accuracy and member trust at once.
```

## Step 5 — Write the one-page discovery brief and get it read back to you

```
CALDERA ENERGY CO-OP -- DISCOVERY BRIEF

Scale:                  ~5,000 residential/small-business installations;
                        telemetry every few minutes per installation
Problem 1 (billing):    Manual CSV export + spreadsheet process; zero
                        automated validation; last known error (Harlan
                        Voss, INV-04821) only caught by luck
Problem 2 (field ops):  No timely visibility into underperforming
                        installations; faults found only via member
                        complaint, weeks after onset
Stakeholders:           Renata Vance (VP, Member Services) -- sponsor
                        Priya Shah (Billing & Finance Manager)
                        Desmond Okafor (Field Operations Manager)
```

Read it back to Renata line by line and get an explicit yes before the next lesson turns this into a testable definition of "correct."

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran discovery with Caldera's Member Services, Billing, and Field Ops leads. The billing problem isn't one bad formula -- it's a manual CSV-to-spreadsheet process with zero automated validation, which just produced an unexplained credit swing on a real member's account (Harlan Voss, INV-04821: $84 to $211.60, traced to a duplicated week of data). Separately, Field Ops has no real-time visibility into failing installations at all. Both point at the same root cause: roughly a million telemetry events a day that nobody's systematically using.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We met with Caldera's VP of Member Services, Billing lead, and Field Ops manager and documented two distinct problems: a billing process that can't validate itself, which just caused a real member billing scare, and zero visibility into equipment that needs maintenance. Nothing gets built yet -- this discovery brief is what the next few lessons turn into a specific, testable plan.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We sat down with Caldera's team after a real member almost lost trust in his bill. The good news: we found the actual root cause, not just one bad number, and it's fixable. We now have a clear, written picture of exactly what's broken before we spend a dollar building anything.

lessons.title: Turning 'Give Us Real Numbers' Into a Testable Billing Definition
lessons.summary: Converting the discovery brief into acceptance criteria specific enough to catch the next Harlan Voss before a member ever has to call.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The discovery meeting gave you a real problem and a forcing event — Harlan Voss's unexplained credit swing — but "give us real numbers" is not yet something a data engineer can build against. This lesson turns that brief into acceptance criteria specific enough that you, Renata Vance, and Priya Shah can all look at a finished billing total and agree, without arguing, whether it's correct.

This is the document every later decision in the series gets checked against. When you choose how raw telemetry gets captured, how it gets cleaned, and what the Gold-layer billing table actually contains, you'll be building against lines in this document — including one acceptance criterion written specifically so Harlan's disputed month, re-run through the finished pipeline, produces exactly $84.00 and nothing else.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a teacher says your book report just needs to be "good." That doesn't tell you anything useful — good how? Long? Have a drawing? Mention the main character? A much better instruction is a checklist: "at least two paragraphs, name the main character, say what happens at the end." Now you and the teacher can both look at the finished report and agree whether it meets the checklist, with no arguing.

That's what we're doing for Caldera's billing numbers. "Give us real numbers" becomes a specific checklist: exactly what counts as a kWh of generation, exactly how a credit gets calculated from it, and exactly how we'd know if the computer ever counted something twice — like it accidentally did for Harlan Voss. Once that checklist exists, anyone can check a bill against it instead of just hoping it's right.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A discovery brief tells you the problem; acceptance criteria tell you how you'll know it's solved, and they only count if they're falsifiable. "The billing numbers should be accurate" is not an acceptance criterion — "the sum of kWh generated for installation INV-04821 across a billing month, reconciled against the raw telemetry count for that installation and month, matches to the kWh, with zero telemetry readings counted more than once" is. The second version is something you can actually go verify with a query; the first is something people will argue about at delivery time.

The sharpest divergence to resolve here is what "generation" even means as a number. Every telemetry reading from an inverter carries a kWh-generated value and a panel-health status; the acceptance criteria have to say explicitly whether a reading flagged as degraded or invalid still counts toward billing (it should not), and — directly because of what happened to Harlan — that no single telemetry reading may ever be counted more than once toward a member's monthly total, no matter how many times it was captured, exported, or reprocessed. That last rule sounds obvious written down this way, but it's exactly the rule the old spreadsheet process had no mechanism to enforce, and it's the rule every later pipeline stage — ingestion, cleaning, and the Gold-layer billing table — has to be able to prove it's honoring, not just assume it is.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull every testable claim out of the discovery brief

Go line by line through the Lesson 1 brief and extract what has to become a criterion:

- Scale: ~5,000 installations, telemetry every few minutes
- Billing trust: currently zero automated validation; last known failure was a duplicated week of data inflating one member's credit
- Field ops visibility: currently zero; deferred to the next lesson's scoping conversation, not solved here
- Stakeholders who have to sign off: Renata Vance, Priya Shah

## Step 2 — Define "generation" precisely, in writing, before anything else

```
GENERATION DEFINITION (v1, pending Priya's written confirmation):

A kWh-generated value counts toward an installation's monthly total
only if:
  1. It comes from a telemetry reading reported by that installation's
     inverter during the billing month in question.
  2. The reading's panel-health status is not flagged as degraded or
     invalid at the time it was reported.
  3. It is counted exactly once -- regardless of how many times the
     underlying event was captured, exported, or reprocessed by any
     system between the inverter and the final billing total.

Net-metering credit = (total qualifying kWh for the month) x
                       (the co-op's published per-kWh credit rate).
```

Rule 3 exists because of Harlan Voss, not in spite of him -- it's the single clause that would have made his disputed month impossible to produce by accident.

## Step 3 — Write acceptance criteria per deliverable, with a verification method attached to each

```
DELIVERABLE: Raw telemetry capture
  AC-1: Every telemetry reading from every installation is captured
        and durably stored, with enough detail to later prove whether
        it was counted once, zero times, or more than once.
  Verification: For any installation and any day, the number of
        stored raw readings must be independently countable and
        auditable against the inverter's expected reporting interval.

DELIVERABLE: Cleaned / curated telemetry
  AC-2: Readings flagged as degraded or invalid at the panel-health
        level are excluded from anything that feeds billing.
  Verification: Spot-query the curated data for a sample installation
        and confirm excluded readings are visibly marked, not silently
        dropped with no trace.

DELIVERABLE: Monthly billing total (Gold layer)
  AC-3: No telemetry reading is ever counted more than once toward a
        monthly total, for any installation, in any month.
  Verification: Reconcile the count of raw readings against the count
        of readings reflected in the billing total for a sample of
        installations and months; the counts must match exactly.
  AC-4: Re-running Harlan Voss's disputed month (INV-04821) through
        the finished pipeline produces exactly $84.00, not $211.60.
  Verification: This is a literal, named regression test -- it either
        produces $84.00 or the pipeline isn't done.
```

## Step 4 — Walk the criteria past Priya and Renata out loud, line by line

```
YOU: AC-4 says if we feed the pipeline Harlan's actual month of data,
     it has to come out to $84.00. Does that match what you both
     believe the correct number was?
PRIYA: Yes -- that's the number I hand-corrected it to.
RENATA: And if a future member's number looks strange, this is what
        we'd check it against?
YOU: Exactly -- that's the whole point of writing it down this
     specifically.
```

## Step 5 — Version it and save it as the contract the rest of the series builds against

Save it as something like `Caldera_V1_Billing_Acceptance_Criteria_v1.docx`, with the approval date noted. Lesson 3 uses this exact document to draw the v1/v2 scope line, and a later lesson in this series proves the finished pipeline against AC-3 and AC-4 directly.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted the discovery brief into testable acceptance criteria: a precise definition of what counts as billable generation, an explicit no-double-counting rule, and a named regression test -- Harlan Voss's disputed month has to resolve to exactly $84.00 once the pipeline is built. Everything from ingestion through the Gold billing table gets checked against these criteria, not against anyone's memory of the kickoff meeting.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've turned 'give us real numbers' into a signed-off checklist with a verification method for every item, including a specific real-world test case from the member complaint that started this project. That means when we say billing is fixed, there's a concrete way to prove it instead of a judgment call.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've written down, in specific and checkable terms, exactly what a correct monthly bill looks like -- including a direct test against the member complaint that got this project started. When this ships, we'll be able to show, not just claim, that it's accurate.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Billing Accuracy Now, Maintenance Alerts Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard, written line around what v1 actually ships, so Desmond's real need for proactive maintenance alerts doesn't quietly turn a billing-trust project into an open-ended one.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have acceptance criteria for correct billing. Before any AWS service gets provisioned, this lesson draws a hard, written line around what v1 actually delivers — and documents, just as explicitly, what's being deliberately deferred. Desmond Okafor's maintenance-visibility problem is just as real as Harlan Voss's billing problem, but solving both perfectly in one pass is how projects quietly grow past their timeline.

This lesson also resolves a subtlety that's easy to miss: the data platform you're about to build for billing — ingesting and cleaning telemetry, and landing a daily per-installation performance table — produces most of what Desmond eventually needs almost as a byproduct. What v1 does *not* include is the active layer on top of it: thresholds, notifications, and an on-call process that actually tells Desmond's team "go roll a truck to this address today."
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're building a treehouse and you promised your friend it would be done by Saturday. On Tuesday, your friend says, "Can it also have a slide, and can it alert me by walkie-talkie whenever a squirrel climbs in?" Both ideas are good, but if you say yes to everything, Saturday isn't happening. The smart move is two lists: "this is in the treehouse we promised by Saturday" and "this is on the list for next time" — and you explain honestly that once you've built the walls and the floor (Saturday's job), adding a walkie-talkie alarm later is actually pretty easy, because the hard part (the treehouse itself) is already done.

That's exactly what's happening with Caldera. Fixing the billing numbers means building a system that watches every solar panel's data closely — and once that system exists, teaching it to also send Desmond's team an alert is a smaller next step, not a brand-new project. But it's still a next step, not part of this one.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is scope management, and the artifact that comes out of it is a scope boundary document, not just a wish list. The subtlety worth naming out loud in this lesson is that v1's billing pipeline and Desmond's eventual maintenance-alerting feature are not unrelated asks competing for the same budget — they share an ingestion and cleaning layer almost entirely. Building a daily per-installation, per-day performance signal (generation totals, a panel-health flag) is nearly free once the telemetry is already flowing and being cleaned for billing purposes. What is *not* free, and what genuinely belongs in a later phase, is the active notification layer: deciding what threshold of degraded readings constitutes "needs a truck roll," building the alerting mechanism itself, and standing up the operational process for who receives and acts on that alert. Conflating "the data exists" with "the feature is built" is exactly the kind of scope creep that quietly turns a billing-trust project into an open-ended one.

The practical skill demonstrated here is handling a legitimate, urgent-sounding request without simply refusing it. Desmond's need is real and arguably more operationally painful than Harlan's billing dispute — but the right response to "can we also get alerts in v1" is never a flat no. It's "yes, and here's what it costs to pull into this phase versus taking it as the very first item in the next one, now that the foundation already supports it cheaply."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List everything on the table that isn't in the v1 billing acceptance criteria

```
MENTIONED IN DISCOVERY, NOT IN THE LESSON 2 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
  - Proactive alerts to Field Operations when an installation is
    underperforming or reporting a degraded panel-health status
  - A field-ops-facing view/dashboard of installation health across
    the whole territory
  - Predictive maintenance scoring (flagging installations likely to
    fail soon, not just ones already failing)
  - A member-facing mobile app showing real-time generation
  - Any form of real-time billing (confirmed out of scope -- monthly
    billing cadence is explicitly what Caldera's net-metering program
    requires, not a technical limitation)
```

## Step 2 — Give each item a real disposition

```
ITEM                                DISPOSITION    WHY
Proactive maintenance alerts        Deferred to v2  Needs threshold design,
                                                     a notification channel, and
                                                     an on-call process Desmond's
                                                     team hasn't defined yet.
Field-ops health dashboard           Deferred to v2  Depends on the alerting
                                                     feature's data shape; design
                                                     it once, not twice.
Predictive maintenance scoring       Deferred to v2  Needs a baseline of reliable
                                                     historical data first, which
                                                     v1 is what creates.
Member-facing mobile app             Rejected (v1)   Outside a data-engineering
                                                     scope entirely; a product/app
                                                     decision, not this project's.
Real-time billing cadence            Rejected        Not a technical gap -- net
                                                     metering is a monthly program
                                                     by design; nightly/batch
                                                     billing data is correct, not
                                                     a compromise.
```

## Step 3 — Name exactly what v1 DOES build, including the part that quietly helps v2 later

```
V1 SCOPE (this series' core build):
  - Real-time capture of inverter telemetry (no gaps, no silent drops)
  - A cleaned, curated, de-duplicated version of that telemetry
  - gold.installation_performance_gold -- one row per installation per
    day: kWh generated, a panel-health flag. Built now because it's a
    natural output of cleaning telemetry for billing anyway -- but
    nothing reads it proactively yet. It is a dataset, not an alert.
  - gold.monthly_billing_gold -- one row per installation per billing
    month: total kWh, net-metering credit. This is what replaces the
    manual spreadsheet process and satisfies Lesson 2's acceptance
    criteria, including the Harlan Voss regression test.
```

## Step 4 — Rehearse the scope-creep conversation before Desmond asks it mid-build

```
DESMOND: If you're already building a table with daily panel-health
         data per installation, can't you just email me when one goes
         bad? That feels like it's basically already done.
YOU:     The data will exist, and that's exactly why v2 will be fast
         once we get there -- we won't be starting from zero. But
         "basically already done" and "done" are different: someone
         still has to decide what counts as bad enough to alert on,
         build the actual notification, and your team needs a process
         for what happens when a text comes in at 2am. Pulling that
         into this phase pushes the billing-trust deadline back. Do
         you want it in v1 with that tradeoff, or as the very first
         thing we build in v2, now that the expensive part is done?
DESMOND: ...First thing in v2. Just don't let the data get built in a
         way that makes v2 harder than it has to be.
YOU:     Noted -- that's exactly why the daily performance table is
         part of v1's design, even though nothing reads it yet.
```

## Step 5 — Get written sign-off on both lists from Renata

Attach the Lesson 2 acceptance criteria and this v1/v2 boundary to one message, and ask Renata Vance for explicit confirmation of both — not a read receipt. This is the document a later lesson in the series reopens when the finished v1 platform ships and the v2 maintenance-alerting backlog gets picked up next.

The billing table satisfies the acceptance criteria and the Harlan Voss regression test; the performance table gets built now because it's a near-free byproduct of cleaning telemetry anyway, but nothing acts on it yet. Proactive alerting, a field-ops dashboard, and predictive scoring are all explicitly deferred to v2, with Desmond's sign-off.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've drawn a clear line between what ships now -- a trustworthy billing pipeline -- and what's next -- proactive maintenance alerts for Field Operations. Desmond's team agreed the data foundation gets built in a way that makes v2 cheap and fast, without pulling v2's actual feature work into this phase's timeline.
workplaceExplanation.executive: This phase fixes the billing trust problem completely. Equally important, we're building the foundation in a way that makes the next phase -- real-time maintenance alerts for the field team -- faster and cheaper once we get to it, instead of starting that from scratch later.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Kinesis, Glue, and Redshift, Not One Bigger Spreadsheet
lessons.summary: Why a serverless streaming-and-lake architecture fits this job, and what each AWS service is -- and isn't -- responsible for.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: which services actually build this thing. For Caldera, the answer is a serverless AWS pipeline — Amazon Kinesis, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3, AWS Glue, and Amazon Redshift — not because they're the only tools that could do this, but because they fit this specific data volume, this team's size, and this budget. This lesson walks through why, and draws a clear boundary around what each service owns, so when something breaks three lessons from now, you already know exactly where to look.

This is also where the exact names you'll use for the rest of the series get fixed: the Kinesis stream `caldera-inverter-telemetry`, the Lambda function `ingest-inverter-events`, the raw lake bucket `caldera-lake-raw`, the Glue Catalog database `caldera_energy`, the curated lake location `caldera-lake-curated`, and the `gold` schema in Redshift. Every later implementation lesson in this series builds against these exact names.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a fire station. A fire alarm going off needs to reach the firefighters in seconds, not get dropped in a mailbox and read next Tuesday. But the station also keeps a big filing cabinet of past incident reports it doesn't need instantly — those can be filed away a little slower, as long as they're filed correctly and nothing gets lost.

Caldera's solar telemetry is a lot like that: it shows up constantly, all day, from 5,000 different places, and some of it eventually needs fast attention (that's the fire-alarm part, coming in a later phase). A single spreadsheet is like trying to run a fire station out of one notebook that someone updates once a month — it was never built to catch things as they happen. So instead we're using a set of tools that are each built for one piece of this: one tool to catch the messages the instant they arrive, one tool to store and organize them, one tool to clean them up, and one tool to hold the final trustworthy numbers everyone reads from.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is a deliberately managed, serverless architecture, and the reasoning matters more than the service names. Caldera's 5,000 installations, each reporting every few minutes, produce well over a million telemetry events a day — a volume and a continuous arrival pattern that a monthly CSV export and a spreadsheet were never designed to handle, and that a traditional scheduled batch job into a relational database would handle only awkwardly. Just as important: Caldera is a small co-op with no dedicated data-platform team, which rules out anything that requires standing infrastructure to patch, scale, or babysit. A serverless, pay-for-what-you-use stack fits both constraints at once.

Each service gets exactly one job. Amazon Kinesis Data Stream `caldera-inverter-telemetry` is the real-time ingestion layer — it exists to receive a continuous, high-volume stream of small events durably and in order, nothing more. The Lambda function `ingest-inverter-events`, triggered by that stream, is the simplest possible consumer: it writes each batch of records as-is into the `caldera-lake-raw` S3 bucket, under an `inverter_events/` prefix partitioned by date — no cleaning, no deduplication, no business logic at all. That's a deliberate design choice, not a shortcut: keeping the ingestion path dumb and fast means a bug in cleaning logic can never cause raw telemetry to be lost, since the unmodified record is already durably in the lake first. An AWS Glue Crawler catalogs that raw location into the Glue Data Catalog database `caldera_energy` as table `raw_inverter_events`, so the data is queryable by schema without anyone hand-writing DDL against a stream of JSON. A Glue ETL job, written in PySpark, is where the real engineering happens — reading `raw_inverter_events`, applying the generation definition and exclusion rules from Lesson 2, and writing curated output to `s3://caldera-lake-curated/inverter_events_clean/`, cataloged as `caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean`. Finally, Amazon Redshift's `gold` schema is the only layer either Caldera team ever queries directly: `gold.installation_performance_gold` and `gold.monthly_billing_gold` are the governed, structured, final answer — not a place where ad hoc cleanup happens. If you ever find the generation-counting logic duplicated between the Glue ETL job and a Redshift query, that's a sign this boundary has blurred, and it's exactly the kind of blurred boundary that makes a dedup bug easy to miss later.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List the actual constraints before picking any service

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - ~5,000 installations x telemetry every few minutes = well over a
    million small events per day, arriving continuously, not in one
    nightly batch
  - Caldera has no dedicated data-platform team -- whatever ships has
    to be manageable without round-the-clock infrastructure babysitting
  - v1's hard requirement is billing trust (Lesson 2's acceptance
    criteria); v2's near-real-time maintenance alerting (Lesson 3) is
    coming later and should not require re-architecting the ingestion
    layer when it arrives
  - Budget fits a co-op, not an enterprise -- pay-for-what-you-use
    beats always-on provisioned infrastructure
```

## Step 2 — Assign exactly one job to each service

```
LAYER                 SERVICE                          RESPONSIBLE FOR                      NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR
Real-time ingestion   Kinesis Data Stream               Durably receiving a continuous       Transformation, storage,
                       "caldera-inverter-telemetry"      stream of telemetry events in order  cleaning, billing logic
Raw landing            Lambda "ingest-inverter-events"   Writing each batch to S3 as-is,      Cleaning, deduplication,
                       -> S3 "caldera-lake-raw"           under inverter_events/, partitioned  typing, business rules
                       (inverter_events/ prefix)          by date -- no transformation at all
Cataloging raw data    Glue Crawler -> Glue Data         Making the raw S3 location            Transformation, cleaning
                       Catalog db "caldera_energy",       queryable by schema
                       table "raw_inverter_events"
Cleaning/curation      Glue ETL job (PySpark) ->         Applying the generation definition    Serving queries directly
                       S3 "caldera-lake-curated/          and exclusion rules from Lesson 2;    to either Caldera team
                       inverter_events_clean/", cataloged  writing a typed, deduplicated,
                       as caldera_energy.                  curated dataset
                       inverter_events_clean
Governed final layer   Redshift schema "gold":           The only layer either Caldera team    Ad hoc cleanup, raw
                       gold.installation_performance_gold  queries directly -- trustworthy,     ingestion logic
                       gold.monthly_billing_gold           structured, final answers
```

## Step 3 — Name the alternatives considered, and why they lost

```
- A bigger, better spreadsheet / Power Query model instead of a real
  pipeline: rejected -- this is literally what caused Harlan Voss's
  disputed month. Scaling the exact process that already failed once
  doesn't fix the root cause, it just delays the next failure.
- Scheduled batch loads into a relational database (no streaming)
  instead of Kinesis: rejected for v1 -- it would technically satisfy
  the billing acceptance criteria today, but it would mean rebuilding
  the ingestion layer from scratch when v2's near-real-time
  maintenance alerting (Lesson 3) arrives. Streaming ingestion now
  costs little extra and avoids that rework later.
- Writing cleaning/dedup logic directly in Lambda at ingest time
  instead of a separate Glue ETL stage: rejected -- it would blur the
  "ingestion is dumb and fast, cleaning is where logic lives" boundary
  that keeps a bug in one stage from threatening raw data durability
  in the other.
- A single all-purpose Redshift table instead of two Gold tables:
  rejected -- daily installation performance and monthly billing are
  genuinely different grains, serving different audiences, which is
  exactly the kind of split a star-schema-style Gold layer is built
  for.
```

## Step 4 — Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We used Kinesis, Lambda, S3, Glue, and Redshift because Caldera's
telemetry volume and continuous arrival pattern outgrew a monthly
spreadsheet the moment it caused a real billing dispute, and because a
small co-op with no dedicated data-platform team needs a managed,
pay-for-what-you-use stack rather than infrastructure to maintain.
Keeping ingestion (Kinesis + Lambda) dumb and fast, cleaning (Glue)
separate and auditable, and the Gold layer in Redshift as the only
thing either team queries directly, means every number either team
sees traces back to one pipeline, not three disconnected processes."
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the stack: Kinesis stream caldera-inverter-telemetry, Lambda ingest-inverter-events writing raw to S3 caldera-lake-raw with zero transformation, a Glue Crawler cataloging it into caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events, a Glue PySpark ETL job producing caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean in caldera-lake-curated, and gold.installation_performance_gold plus gold.monthly_billing_gold in Redshift as the only layer either Caldera team queries directly. Each stage has exactly one job, which is what keeps a bug in one from threatening data in another.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've picked a managed, pay-for-what-you-use set of AWS services sized for Caldera's actual data volume and small team, instead of scaling the spreadsheet process that already caused a real billing dispute. The architecture is also built so the maintenance-alerting feature we deferred to v2 won't require rebuilding the ingestion layer when we get there.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're building this on managed AWS services that scale with your actual data volume and don't require you to hire a team to maintain servers. This replaces the spreadsheet process that already caused a billing scare, and it's designed so the maintenance-alert feature you want next doesn't mean starting over.

lessons.title: Designing the Raw-to-Curated-to-Gold Data Flow on S3
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding the raw, curated, and gold layers across S3 and Redshift -- grain, ownership, and why ops and billing each need their own Gold table.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With the Kinesis/Glue/Redshift stack chosen, this lesson whiteboards the actual shape of Caldera's data lake before a single bucket exists. Telemetry will move through three layers: **raw** (`s3://caldera-lake-raw/inverter_events/`), **curated** (`s3://caldera-lake-curated/inverter_events_clean/`), and **gold** (two tables in Redshift's `gold` schema). This lesson defines the grain of each layer, who's allowed to touch it, and why the two Gold tables -- one for the maintenance team, one for billing -- have to stay separate rather than living as one wide table.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a commercial kitchen with a loading dock, a prep station, and a pass-through window. Deliveries land on the dock exactly as the truck brought them -- nobody sorts or inspects anything yet, they just get logged and stacked. At the prep station, a cook actually washes, chops, and checks everything, throwing out anything that's gone bad. Only then does finished food go out two different windows -- one tray for the kitchen manager checking on table turnover, a completely different plate for the cashier ringing up the bill.

Caldera's data lake works the same way. Raw telemetry lands untouched, like the loading dock. The curated layer is the prep station, where real cleaning happens. And Gold is two separate "windows" -- one for the maintenance team checking on inverter health, one for the billing system calculating what each household owes or is credited.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The raw layer exists purely to be a faithful, replayable record of what Kinesis actually delivered -- it is append-only, untyped, and never edited or deleted. That matters more than it sounds: Kinesis and Lambda guarantee at-least-once delivery, which means `ingest-inverter-events` can legitimately write the same batch to S3 more than once after a retry. Raw is deliberately allowed to contain that duplication. Fighting it at the ingestion layer would add real complexity to solve a problem that's cheaper to solve downstream, where a proper key can identify and collapse duplicates deliberately -- so raw's only job is "what arrived," not "what's correct."

Curated is where correctness actually gets built: casting raw string fields to real types, normalizing timestamps, and collapsing duplicate deliveries down to one row per inverter reading. Gold then splits into two tables specifically because they serve two audiences with different stakes and different change-management needs. `gold.installation_performance_gold` is a daily, ops-facing table -- a maintenance coordinator needs to see yesterday's underperforming installations today, not at the end of a billing cycle. `gold.monthly_billing_gold` is a monthly, finance-facing table that feeds member-facing dollar figures directly -- the exact kind of number that produced Caldera's real billing dispute. Keeping them as separate tables means a schema change made for the maintenance dashboard can never silently shift a number that ends up on an invoice.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the grain statement for every layer, before sketching anything

```
RAW GRAIN:      One S3 object = one Lambda invocation's batch of
                inverter readings, exactly as Kinesis delivered them.
                No dedup, no typing, no deletion, ever.
CURATED GRAIN:  One row = one inverter's reading at one timestamp,
                cleaned, typed, and deduplicated against raw's
                at-least-once deliveries.
GOLD GRAIN (ops):      One row = one installation, one calendar day.
GOLD GRAIN (billing):  One row = one installation, one calendar month.
```

## Step 2 — Whiteboard the raw layer

```
s3://caldera-lake-raw/inverter_events/
  dt=2026-10-23/
    hr=14/
      ingest-inverter-events-<shard-id>-<sequence>.json
```

- Written directly by `ingest-inverter-events`, with no transformation at all
- Partitioned by date (and hour) purely so the Glue Crawler and later ad-hoc queries can prune -- not for cleanup
- Append-only and immutable: once an object lands here, it is never edited or deleted. Raw's entire value is being a trustworthy, replayable source -- if a downstream bug is ever found, raw is what lets the pipeline be re-run correctly from the beginning instead of from already-corrupted data

## Step 3 — Whiteboard the curated layer

```
s3://caldera-lake-curated/inverter_events_clean/
  dt=2026-10-23/
    part-00000.snappy.parquet
```

Typed schema, written by the Glue ETL job reading `caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events`:

```
installation_id      string
inverter_id           string
reading_timestamp     timestamp
voltage_v             double
current_a             double
power_output_kw       double
cumulative_kwh        double
status_code           string
```

Parquet instead of JSON -- columnar, smaller, and the format Redshift and Glue read fastest. This is the layer where real cleaning happens: type casting, timezone normalization, quarantining malformed readings, and collapsing duplicate deliveries to one row per inverter per timestamp. Exactly how that collapsing works is the Glue ETL job's own design decision, built in a later lesson -- this whiteboard only fixes the contract that job has to satisfy. Cataloged as `caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean`.

## Step 4 — Whiteboard the two Gold tables, and why there are two

```sql
-- gold.installation_performance_gold -- the OPS/MAINTENANCE table
installation_id         VARCHAR(20)
performance_date        DATE
total_kwh_generated     DECIMAL(10,2)
avg_power_output_kw     DECIMAL(10,2)
health_flag             VARCHAR(20)   -- NORMAL / UNDERPERFORMING / OFFLINE

-- gold.monthly_billing_gold -- the BILLING/FINANCE table
installation_id         VARCHAR(20)
billing_month           DATE
total_kwh_generated     DECIMAL(10,2)
net_metering_credit_usd DECIMAL(10,2)
```

`installation_performance_gold` answers "is this installation healthy right now" for the field team. `monthly_billing_gold` answers "what does this household owe or get credited" for finance, and feeds member invoices directly. Different grain, different audience, different stakes -- a new health metric added for maintenance next quarter should never be able to touch a column billing depends on.

## Step 5 — Map each layer to who touches it and how often

```
LAYER                                 TOUCHED BY                 CADENCE
raw (S3)                              ingest-inverter-events      continuous, per batch
curated (S3 + Glue Catalog)           Glue ETL job                 scheduled run
gold.installation_performance_gold    Ops/maintenance dashboards    daily refresh
gold.monthly_billing_gold             Billing/finance, invoices      monthly refresh
```

## Step 6 — Draw the end-to-end flow as one line

```
Kinesis (caldera-inverter-telemetry)
  -> Lambda (ingest-inverter-events)
  -> S3 raw (caldera-lake-raw/inverter_events/)
  -> Glue Crawler -> Glue Catalog (caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events)
  -> Glue ETL job
  -> S3 curated (caldera-lake-curated/inverter_events_clean/)
  -> Glue Catalog (caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean)
  -> Redshift load
  -> gold.installation_performance_gold / gold.monthly_billing_gold
```

Every lesson from here through the end of implementation builds one segment of this line -- and every segment's design has to trace back to the grain statement in Step 1.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded the data flow before creating a single bucket: raw stays append-only and is allowed to contain duplicates from Kinesis/Lambda's at-least-once delivery, curated is where real cleaning and dedup collapsing happens, and gold splits into two Redshift tables -- daily installation_performance_gold for ops, monthly monthly_billing_gold for billing -- so a schema change on one can never silently touch the other.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped out exactly how inverter data moves from the moment it lands to the two reports people actually use -- a daily health view for the field team and a monthly billing number for finance -- before any infrastructure gets built. That separation is what protects the billing number from getting tangled up with unrelated operational changes.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before building anything, we planned how raw sensor data becomes a trustworthy billing number, with the maintenance team's daily view kept completely separate from the monthly number that goes on member invoices. That separation is part of how we prevent another billing dispute like the one that brought us in.

lessons.title: Planning the Terraform-Provisioned AWS Infrastructure
lessons.summary: Planning the Terraform module layout, state backend, and CI plan gate for every AWS resource this platform needs.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With the raw-to-curated-to-gold data flow whiteboarded, this lesson plans how the AWS resources that flow depends on actually get created: S3 buckets, the Kinesis stream, the Lambda function, the Glue database/crawler/job, and the Redshift cluster/schema, all provisioned through Terraform rather than clicked together by hand in the console. We're deciding the module layout, the remote state backend, and a CI plan step before a single `.tf` file exists -- so Lesson 8's first real `terraform apply` lands on a structure that was actually designed, not improvised.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a construction crew about to build a house. Before anyone pours concrete, there's a blueprint that labels exactly which folder of drawings covers the plumbing, which covers the electrical, and which covers the foundation -- and a filing cabinet, locked, that holds the one official copy of those drawings so two crews never work from two different versions by accident.

Terraform is how we build Caldera's AWS resources from a blueprint instead of by hand, one click at a time. This lesson plans the folders (one per AWS service), the locked filing cabinet (where Terraform remembers what it already built), and a rule that any change to the blueprint gets checked by a second person before it's allowed to actually change anything real.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The module boundary we're drawing mirrors the AWS service boundary, not an arbitrary folder split: one Terraform module per S3, Kinesis, Lambda, Glue, and Redshift, each with its own typed inputs and outputs, wired together from a root module per environment (`envs/dev`, `envs/prod`). That boundary matters because these resources have genuinely different lifecycles -- the S3 buckets and the Redshift cluster are long-lived and rarely change shape, while the Lambda function's code and the Glue job's script change far more often; keeping them in separate modules means a frequent Lambda deploy never has to re-plan the Redshift cluster.

Remote state in S3, locked through DynamoDB, is what lets this be a team process instead of a file on one person's laptop -- without it, two people running `terraform apply` at the same time can corrupt each other's state or double-provision a resource. The CI plan step closes the loop: every pull request runs `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate`, and `terraform plan`, and a human reviews the actual plan output -- which resources get created, changed, or destroyed -- before approving the merge. `terraform apply` deliberately never runs inside that same automated workflow; the gate here is "prove the plan is correct and show a human exactly what changes," the same discipline a dbt pull request enforces with `dbt build` and `dbt test` before anything reaches production.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Lay out the repo and module structure

```
infra/
  envs/
    dev/
      main.tf
      variables.tf
      backend.tf
    prod/
      main.tf
      variables.tf
      backend.tf
  modules/
    s3_data_lake/
      main.tf
      variables.tf
      outputs.tf
    kinesis_stream/
    lambda_ingest/
    glue_catalog/
    redshift_cluster/
```

One module per AWS service boundary. `dev` and `prod` share the same module code and only differ in the variables each environment passes in -- never a copy-pasted fork of the module itself.

## Step 2 — Plan the remote state backend first

```hcl
# infra/envs/dev/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "caldera-terraform-state"
    key            = "dev/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "caldera-terraform-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
```

`caldera-terraform-state` and `caldera-terraform-locks` get created once, outside this Terraform config, before any environment's `terraform init` ever runs against them -- state storage can't depend on the infrastructure it's tracking.

## Step 3 — Sketch each module's inputs and outputs

```
module "s3_data_lake"     variables: raw_bucket_name, curated_bucket_name
                          outputs:   raw_bucket_arn, curated_bucket_arn

module "kinesis_stream"    variables: stream_name, shard_count
                          outputs:   stream_arn

module "lambda_ingest"     variables: function_name, raw_bucket_name,
                                       kinesis_stream_arn
                          outputs:   function_arn

module "glue_catalog"      variables: database_name, raw_bucket_name,
                                       curated_bucket_name
                          outputs:   database_name

module "redshift_cluster"  variables: cluster_identifier, schema_name
                          outputs:   cluster_endpoint
```

Every module only knows about the inputs it actually needs -- `redshift_cluster` never references an S3 bucket name directly; the root module wires one module's outputs into another module's variables.

## Step 4 — Wire the modules together in the root module

```hcl
# infra/envs/dev/main.tf
module "s3_data_lake" {
  source              = "../../modules/s3_data_lake"
  raw_bucket_name      = "caldera-lake-raw"
  curated_bucket_name  = "caldera-lake-curated"
}

module "kinesis_stream" {
  source      = "../../modules/kinesis_stream"
  stream_name = "caldera-inverter-telemetry"
  shard_count = 2
}

module "lambda_ingest" {
  source             = "../../modules/lambda_ingest"
  function_name      = "ingest-inverter-events"
  raw_bucket_name    = module.s3_data_lake.raw_bucket_arn
  kinesis_stream_arn = module.kinesis_stream.stream_arn
}

module "glue_catalog" {
  source              = "../../modules/glue_catalog"
  database_name        = "caldera_energy"
  raw_bucket_name      = module.s3_data_lake.raw_bucket_arn
  curated_bucket_name  = module.s3_data_lake.curated_bucket_arn
}

module "redshift_cluster" {
  source             = "../../modules/redshift_cluster"
  cluster_identifier = "caldera-dw"
  schema_name        = "gold"
}
```

## Step 5 — Plan the CI gate: plan on every PR, apply only after review

```yaml
# .github/workflows/terraform_plan.yml
name: Terraform Plan
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev fmt -check
      - run: terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev init
      - run: terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev validate
      - run: terraform -chdir=infra/envs/dev plan -no-color
```

`terraform apply` is deliberately not in this workflow -- CI's job is to prove the plan is valid and show a human reviewer exactly what will change. Apply happens from a second, manually-triggered workflow only after that plan has been reviewed.

## Step 6 — Lock the naming convention down now

```
S3 buckets:       caldera-lake-raw, caldera-lake-curated
Kinesis stream:   caldera-inverter-telemetry
Lambda function:  ingest-inverter-events
Glue database:    caldera_energy
Redshift cluster: caldera-dw, schema gold
```

Every later lesson in this series refers to these exact names, as Terraform variables -- locking them here means nobody has to guess which bucket a given Glue job reads from six lessons from now.

## Step 7 — Decide how dev and prod diverge, in variables, not in module code

```hcl
# infra/envs/prod/terraform.tfvars
raw_bucket_name     = "caldera-lake-raw-prod"
curated_bucket_name = "caldera-lake-curated-prod"
shard_count         = 2
cluster_identifier  = "caldera-dw-prod"
```

`dev` and `prod` call the exact same five modules with different `.tfvars` files -- the only thing that changes between environments is the values passed in, never the Terraform code itself. That's what keeps a change tested in `dev` guaranteed to behave the same way once it's applied to `prod`, instead of discovering a module drifted between the two environments the hard way.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the Terraform module layout before writing a resource block: one module per AWS service boundary (S3, Kinesis, Lambda, Glue, Redshift), a shared remote state backend in S3 with DynamoDB locking, and a CI workflow that runs terraform plan on every pull request without ever auto-applying. Naming conventions for every resource are locked now so later lessons never have to guess.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've designed how the infrastructure gets built and reviewed before any of it exists -- every change to the AWS environment will go through a pull request with a visible plan output, the same discipline we'd expect from any production system.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The cloud infrastructure for this platform will be built from code, reviewed before anything changes, and named consistently from day one -- that's what makes it maintainable by this team long after the initial build, not just today.

lessons.title: Planning the Kinesis and Lambda Ingestion Path for Inverter Telemetry
lessons.summary: Sizing Kinesis shards and Lambda batching against ~5,000 installations' real telemetry volume, with an end-to-end latency target.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson plans the actual ingestion path's real-world sizing: how many shards `caldera-inverter-telemetry` needs, what partition key keeps each inverter's readings in order, how `ingest-inverter-events` batches records off the stream, and what end-to-end latency target the whole path should hit -- all worked out against Caldera's real installation count before any of it is provisioned in Lesson 8.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about toll booths on a highway. Before building any booths, you'd count how many cars actually drive through per minute, so you know whether one lane is plenty or you need three. You'd also decide how long a toll both waits to open the gate for a cluster of cars arriving close together, instead of swinging it open and shut for every single car.

That's what we're doing here with Caldera's data highway. We count how many telemetry messages are actually coming in every second from 5,000 solar installations, decide how many "lanes" (shards) that really needs, and plan how the toll booth (Lambda) groups cars together before processing them, so nothing backs up and nothing gets dropped.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Shard sizing has to start from the actual numbers, not a guess. A Kinesis shard supports up to 1,000 records/second or 1 MB/second of writes, whichever limit hits first -- Caldera's real volume needs to be measured against both before a shard count is chosen. The partition key matters just as much as the count: keying on `installation_id` keeps every inverter's readings in order on one consistent shard for its entire lifetime, which later ETL and dedup logic can rely on instead of reassembling order from scattered, out-of-sequence records.

The Lambda event source mapping settings -- batch size, batching window, parallelization factor, reserved concurrency -- are the other half of this plan, and they trade off latency against invocation cost and ordering guarantees. A parallelization factor above 1 would let Lambda process multiple batches from the same shard concurrently, which increases throughput but breaks the in-order guarantee `installation_id`-keyed partitioning was chosen to preserve -- so we accept lower per-shard parallelism here deliberately. Finally, Kinesis and Lambda's at-least-once delivery model means a retried batch can be written to S3 more than once; this lesson names that tradeoff explicitly and accepts it at the ingestion layer, on the understanding that resolving duplicates is a downstream job's responsibility, not this one's.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Compute the real throughput before picking a shard count

```
~5,000 installations, each inverter reporting one telemetry reading
every 5 minutes:

  5,000 readings / 300 seconds   = ~16.7 readings/second
  Average payload size (JSON)    = ~0.5 KB
  Sustained write throughput     = ~16.7 x 0.5 KB = ~8.4 KB/second
```

A single Kinesis shard supports up to 1,000 records/second or 1 MB/second of writes. At ~17 records/second and ~8 KB/second, Caldera's entire current fleet uses roughly 2% of one shard's write capacity.

## Step 2 — Decide shard count and partition key

```
SHARD COUNT:    2
PARTITION KEY:  installation_id
```

Two shards, not one, for reasons that have nothing to do with today's raw throughput:

- **Growth headroom.** Two shards absorb roughly 10x growth -- up to ~50,000 installations at this reporting cadence -- before a resharding operation is needed.
- **Parallel consumption.** Each shard gets its own Lambda event source mapping, processed independently -- a slow or retrying batch on one shard never blocks the other shard's consumer.

Keying on `installation_id` keeps every inverter's readings in order, on one shard, for its whole lifetime -- important later, because downstream dedup logic can assume one installation's readings arrive in sequence rather than scattered across shards.

## Step 3 — Plan the Lambda event source mapping settings

```
Batch size:              100 records
Max batching window:     30 seconds
Parallelization factor:   1   (preserve per-shard ordering)
Reserved concurrency:     10
On-failure destination:  SQS dead-letter queue (caldera-ingest-dlq)
Retry attempts:           3, then route to DLQ
```

A 30-second batching window means `ingest-inverter-events` never waits longer than half a minute to flush a partial batch, even during a quiet stretch, and a batch of 100 small telemetry records is small enough that a single invocation finishes well under a second once it's writing to S3.

## Step 4 — Set the end-to-end latency budget

```
Inverter reads & transmits          -> up to a few seconds (device-side)
PutRecord to Kinesis                -> sub-second
Shard-to-Lambda trigger latency     -> typically 1-5 seconds
Batch window wait (worst case)      -> up to 30 seconds
Lambda execution (S3 PutObject)     -> under 1 second
TOTAL TARGET: under 2 minutes from inverter transmission to a
              readable object in caldera-lake-raw
```

Two minutes is deliberately generous -- nothing downstream of raw needs sub-minute freshness, since both Gold tables are built from a scheduled Glue ETL run, not a live stream read. This budget only protects one promise: that "most recent data in raw" reliably means "within the last couple of minutes."

## Step 5 — Accept the at-least-once tradeoff in writing, now

Kinesis and Lambda both guarantee **at-least-once** delivery, not exactly-once. A Lambda retry after a transient failure -- a throttle, a timeout, a cold start that runs past its window -- can cause the same batch of records to be written to S3 more than once. We accept that tradeoff deliberately at the ingestion layer rather than engineering it away here: building exactly-once delivery into `ingest-inverter-events` itself adds real complexity to solve a problem that's cheaper to solve downstream, where duplicate raw objects can be identified and collapsed against a proper key. That resolution belongs to a later lesson -- this lesson's job is only to name the tradeoff honestly before anything gets built on top of it.

## Step 6 — Set a revisit trigger instead of guessing later

```
REVISIT SHARD COUNT WHEN:
  - Sustained throughput exceeds ~50% of provisioned capacity
  - Installation count approaches 25,000-30,000 at the current
    5-minute reporting cadence
  - Reporting cadence itself changes (e.g. 1-minute telemetry,
    a 5x throughput increase on its own)
```

Provisioned mode, with a documented revisit trigger, keeps costs predictable while Caldera's volume is this far under any real ceiling -- Kinesis On-Demand mode is a fair reconsideration only if growth or cadence changes enough to make manual resharding a frequent chore.

Also documented, in writing, that at-least-once delivery can produce duplicate raw writes on a Lambda retry -- a tradeoff we're accepting here and resolving downstream, not fighting at the ingestion layer.

lessons.title: Provisioning the AWS Infrastructure With Terraform
lessons.summary: The first real AWS infrastructure: S3 buckets, the Kinesis stream, the Glue database, and an empty Redshift gold schema, provisioned with real Terraform.

We're provisioning the skeleton planned in Lessons 5 through 7: the two S3 buckets (`caldera-lake-raw`, `caldera-lake-curated`), the Kinesis stream (`caldera-inverter-telemetry`, 2 shards), the Glue database (`caldera_energy`), and a Redshift cluster with an empty `gold` schema inside it -- no tables yet, no Lambda function yet, no crawler yet. lessons.explainSimple:

Nobody's hanging drywall yet -- today is the day the foundation gets poured and the empty shell of the building goes up, exactly matching the blueprint from the planning meetings. Nothing inside it works yet, but for the first time, it's a real building you could walk into, not just a drawing.

lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson executes the module layout from Lesson 6 against the shard count and naming decisions from Lesson 7, and nothing more. The S3 module adds versioning and a public-access block to both buckets from the start -- raw's immutability promise from Lesson 5 is only real if an accidental overwrite can actually be recovered, which versioning provides and a block-public-access setting protects from outside interference entirely. The Redshift module is the one place this lesson has to step outside pure declarative Terraform: the AWS provider has no native resource for "a schema inside Redshift," so creating `gold` requires a single `null_resource` with a `local-exec` provisioner running one `psql` statement after the cluster is reachable -- an intentionally small, visible exception to an otherwise fully declarative module, not a pattern to repeat casually elsewhere.

Everything here is provisioned in isolation from the pipeline logic that will eventually use it. The Glue database exists with no crawler and no tables registered in it yet; the Kinesis stream exists with no Lambda function consuming it yet; the Redshift cluster has an empty schema with no `installation_performance_gold` or `monthly_billing_gold` tables yet. That sequencing is deliberate -- infrastructure that holds data should exist and be verified before the logic that populates it is layered on top, the same way a warehouse gets built before the trucks start arriving.
