Mistakes get caught in minutes on the proposed change, not after they've reached production.

lessons.title: Adding Monitoring and Alerting to the Pipeline
lessons.summary: Wiring CloudWatch alarms on the Lambda's error rate and the Kinesis stream's iterator age, plus an SNS alert when the Step Functions state machine fails a step, so pipeline trouble reaches a human before it reaches Finance.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
CI now protects the code; nothing yet watches the pipeline while it's actually running. This lesson adds that: a CloudWatch alarm on `ingest-inverter-events`'s Lambda error rate, a second CloudWatch alarm on the `caldera-inverter-telemetry` Kinesis stream's iterator age — the standard metric for "how far behind is the consumer falling" — and an SNS topic, `caldera-pipeline-alerts`, that fires the moment the Step Functions state machine fails a step, all defined in the same Terraform this pipeline already lives in.

This is also the piece that makes Lesson 15's investigation possible at all. Without monitoring, a double-counted billing month gets discovered by Finance weeks later, from a bill a co-op member disputes. With it, the on-call engineer has a real shot at catching the Lambda retrying or the consumer falling behind on the day it happens — before it ever reaches `monthly_billing_gold`.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a smoke detector in a kitchen. It doesn't put out the fire — it just makes sure someone finds out immediately instead of discovering it an hour later. This lesson installs three smoke detectors: one that notices if the program reading solar data keeps crashing, one that notices if that program starts falling behind on reading the incoming data, and one that notices if the robot in charge of running the whole nightly process hits a step it can't finish.

Every detector is wired to the same alarm bell — an email that goes straight to whoever's on call — so nobody has to keep checking a screen all day hoping nothing broke.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Three specific, standard signals get wired to one alerting path here, each chosen because it catches a different failure mode before it becomes a data-quality incident.

The Lambda `Errors` metric on `ingest-inverter-events`, summed over a short window and alarmed above a low absolute threshold, catches outright failures — a malformed payload, a downstream S3 permission problem, a timeout. The Kinesis `GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds` metric, specifically, is the standard way to detect a struggling *consumer* rather than a struggling *producer*: it measures the age of the oldest unprocessed record still sitting in the shard, so a rising iterator age means Lambda is falling behind the stream — exactly the condition under which Lambda's internal retry behavior (the mechanism Lesson 16 traces a real bug back to) becomes more likely to fire. Both alarms publish to the same SNS topic, `caldera-pipeline-alerts`, which also receives a notification the moment the Step Functions state machine orchestrating the Glue job and downstream loads reports a failed execution, via a CloudWatch alarm on that state machine's `ExecutionsFailed` metric.

None of these three signals, alone, proves a billing number is wrong — that's a data-quality question CloudWatch can't answer directly. What they buy is time: a human finding out about Lambda retries or consumer lag on the day it happens, rather than reconstructing it weeks later from a disputed invoice, which is exactly the gap Lesson 15 and 16 walk through closing after the fact.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide what "unhealthy" means for each component, in numbers

```
Lambda (ingest-inverter-events):  Errors >= 1 over any 5-minute window
                                   -> page on-call, don't wait for a
                                   percentage threshold at this volume.
Kinesis (caldera-inverter-telemetry):
  GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds average > 60000 (1 minute) for
  2 consecutive 1-minute periods -> consumer is falling behind.
Step Functions state machine:     ExecutionsFailed >= 1 over any
                                   5-minute window -> a run didn't
                                   complete; investigate immediately.
```

## Step 2 — Create the SNS topic in Terraform

```hcl
# infra/monitoring.tf
resource "aws_sns_topic" "pipeline_alerts" {
  name = "caldera-pipeline-alerts"
}

resource "aws_sns_topic_subscription" "oncall_email" {
  topic_arn = aws_sns_topic.pipeline_alerts.arn
  protocol  = "email"
  endpoint  = var.oncall_alert_email
}
```

## Step 3 — Alarm on the Lambda's error rate

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "ingest_lambda_errors" {
  alarm_name          = "caldera-ingest-inverter-events-errors"
  namespace           = "AWS/Lambda"
  metric_name         = "Errors"
  dimensions          = { FunctionName = "ingest-inverter-events" }
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 300
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
  treat_missing_data  = "notBreaching"
  alarm_actions       = [aws_sns_topic.pipeline_alerts.arn]
}
```

## Step 4 — Alarm on Kinesis iterator age (consumer lag)

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "stream_iterator_age" {
  alarm_name          = "caldera-inverter-telemetry-iterator-age"
  namespace           = "AWS/Kinesis"
  metric_name         = "GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds"
  dimensions          = { StreamName = "caldera-inverter-telemetry" }
  statistic           = "Average"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods   = 2
  threshold           = 60000
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
  alarm_actions       = [aws_sns_topic.pipeline_alerts.arn]
}
```

A rising iterator age is the earliest warning that Lambda is behind the stream — well before a human would otherwise notice anything.

## Step 5 — Alarm on Step Functions execution failures

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "state_machine_failures" {
  alarm_name          = "caldera-pipeline-state-machine-failures"
  namespace           = "AWS/States"
  metric_name         = "ExecutionsFailed"
  dimensions          = { StateMachineArn = aws_sfn_state_machine.caldera_pipeline.arn }
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 300
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
  treat_missing_data  = "notBreaching"
  alarm_actions       = [aws_sns_topic.pipeline_alerts.arn]
}
```

## Step 6 — Confirm the alarms fire, don't just trust the Terraform

Manually publish a malformed record to the Kinesis stream to force a Lambda error, and separately stop the Step Functions state machine's Glue step mid-run from the console. Confirm both CloudWatch alarms transition to `ALARM` and the on-call email actually arrives — a Terraform `apply` that succeeds proves the alarm resource exists, not that it works.

## Step 7 — Write the one-line runbook for each alarm

```
Lambda errors alarm      -> Check CloudWatch Logs for ingest-inverter-events
                             first; look for a malformed payload or an S3
                             permissions error. If errors cluster right
                             after a deploy, suspect the new code, not AWS.
Iterator age alarm       -> Check Lambda concurrency and recent error rate
                             first -- a struggling consumer, not usually the
                             stream itself, is almost always the cause. A
                             sustained climb (not a brief spike) also means
                             Lambda may be retrying failed batches, which is
                             exactly the condition Lesson 16 traces a real
                             data bug back to.
State machine failures   -> Open the failed execution in the Step Functions
                             console; the failed state name tells you
                             exactly which step (Glue job, Redshift load)
                             to look at first, before digging into any
                             underlying service's own logs.
```

A runbook line per alarm turns a 2 a.m. page into a five-minute first step instead of a cold start — and ties the iterator-age alarm specifically to the kind of retry behavior this series later finds a real production bug hiding inside.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Added three CloudWatch alarms — Lambda Errors on ingest-inverter-events, Kinesis IteratorAgeMilliseconds on caldera-inverter-telemetry for consumer lag, and ExecutionsFailed on the Step Functions state machine — all publishing to one SNS topic with an on-call email subscription, defined in the same Terraform as the rest of the pipeline. Verified each alarm fires for real, not just that the Terraform applied cleanly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The pipeline now pages someone automatically the moment the data stops flowing correctly, instead of relying on someone noticing a problem after the fact. We tested each alarm by actually breaking something on purpose and confirming the alert arrived.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've added automatic alerts so our team finds out the same day something goes wrong with the data pipeline, rather than finding out weeks later from a billing complaint. This is a standard safeguard for production systems handling real customer data.

lessons.title: Billing Flags a Monthly Total That's Too High
lessons.summary: Caldera's billing team flags an August total that looks too high for a batch of installations — tracing the number layer by layer, from raw S3 through Curated to Gold, instead of assuming a meter malfunction.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Caldera's billing coordinator, Renata Flores, flags something in the August 2026 run of `gold.monthly_billing_gold`: a batch of installations around installation `INST-04821` are showing kWh totals noticeably higher than their own twelve-month history — in some cases close to double. The easy, wrong move is to assume the hardware is at fault: a miscalibrated inverter, a meter glitch. This lesson resists that instinct and instead verifies the number the same way any pipeline bug gets verified — pull the exact raw data for one specific installation and trace it, layer by layer, through `raw_inverter_events`, `inverter_events_clean`, and `monthly_billing_gold`, until you can say precisely where the number stops matching what should be true.

What the investigation finds is a mismatch that shows up one layer earlier than billing math itself: `inverter_events_clean`, the table every billing number is supposed to be built from *after* cleanup and deduplication, is carrying more rows for this installation and month than it should — which means the problem isn't a bad formula in Gold, it's bad input arriving at Gold already doubled.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a vending machine that's supposed to count each coin once, but a customer's receipt says they spent twice as much as the coins they actually have in hand. Before blaming the customer's wallet, you'd want to check the machine's coin counter itself — did it actually see each coin twice?

That's this lesson. Before assuming a solar panel is broken, we check every step the data takes on its way to the bill: the raw readings, the cleaned-up pile they get turned into, and the final total. It turns out the "cleaned-up pile" already has some readings counted twice — before the final bill is even calculated.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is pipeline-bug triage applied under pressure from a business stakeholder, and the discipline that matters is resisting the fastest-sounding explanation — hardware — in favor of verifying each layer independently against the one before it. Renata's complaint names a symptom (a number too high) but not a cause, and "the meter is broken" is unfalsifiable from the billing report alone; it requires physically inspecting hardware that may not be broken at all.

Instead, the investigation starts from Caldera's own architecture and checks it in order: `s3://caldera-lake-raw/inverter_events/`, queried through the `caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events` Glue table, is the ground truth of what the inverter actually reported — if raw data for `INST-04821` in August looks normal (a reading roughly every few minutes, plausible kWh values), the hardware is very likely not at fault. `caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean` is supposed to be raw, deduplicated — so its row count for the same installation and month should be less than or equal to raw's, never more, and should match the installation's expected reporting cadence for the month. `gold.monthly_billing_gold` is a sum built *from* Clean, so if Clean is already wrong, Gold's formula doesn't need to be wrong at all for the final number to be wrong.

Checking in that order turns up the actual discrepancy one layer earlier than Renata's complaint pointed: Clean has more rows for this installation and month than Raw's distinct reading count would predict, which is only possible if the Glue ETL's deduplication step — the one specifically responsible for collapsing exactly this kind of duplicate — let something through it shouldn't have.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Get the exact scope from Renata, not a vague "it's too high"

```
Renata: "INST-04821 billed 1,842 kWh for August. Its trailing
         twelve-month average is around 930. A few dozen other
         installations in the same batch look similarly doubled —
         I'll send the full list, but let's nail down one first."
```

One specific installation, one specific month, one specific comparison point — exactly what's needed to trace, not a general impression.

## Step 2 — Check raw first: is the hardware even plausible as the cause?

```sql
-- Athena, against the Glue Catalog
SELECT count(*) AS row_count,
       min(reading_timestamp) AS first_reading,
       max(reading_timestamp) AS last_reading
FROM caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821'
  AND reading_timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-08-01' AND TIMESTAMP '2026-08-31 23:59:59';
-- row_count: 8,924   (roughly one reading every 5 minutes for 31 days -- normal cadence)
```

8,924 raw readings at a normal reporting cadence, with normal-looking kWh values per reading, rules out "the inverter is sending garbage." Whatever is wrong, it isn't the hardware.

## Step 3 — Check Clean: should have fewer or equal rows than Raw, never more

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS row_count,
       count(DISTINCT event_id) AS distinct_event_ids
FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821'
  AND reading_timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-08-01' AND TIMESTAMP '2026-08-31 23:59:59';
-- row_count: 9,003        distinct_event_ids: 8,924
```

This is the number that should stop everyone cold: `inverter_events_clean` is supposed to be deduplicated, yet it has **79 more rows than distinct `event_id` values** for this installation and month. A table whose entire job is removing duplicates is carrying duplicates.

## Step 4 — Confirm it: find one duplicated reading by hand

```sql
SELECT event_id, count(*) AS n
FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821'
  AND reading_timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-08-01' AND TIMESTAMP '2026-08-31 23:59:59'
GROUP BY event_id
HAVING count(*) > 1
LIMIT 5;
-- event_id                               n
-- 7f3e2b9a-...-c112                      2
-- 7f3e2b9a-...-c112 appears TWICE in a table that already ran a
-- dropDuplicates step.
```

The same `event_id` — the one field guaranteed unique on every raw record — shows up twice in the supposedly-deduplicated table. That's not a hardware problem and not a formula problem in Gold; it's a dedup step that didn't catch everything it was supposed to.

## Step 5 — Trace the dollar (kWh) impact through to Gold before closing this lesson

```sql
SELECT installation_id, billing_month, total_kwh
FROM gold.monthly_billing_gold
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821' AND billing_month = '2026-08-01';
-- total_kwh: 1,842.6
```

Summing just the 79 duplicated readings' `kwh_interval` values accounts for almost exactly the gap between 1,842.6 and the ~930 historical average — confirming Gold's arithmetic is fine; it's faithfully summing rows that shouldn't all exist.

## Step 6 — Name exactly what's proven, and what isn't yet

```
PROVEN: Raw data for INST-04821 in August is normal -- hardware is not
        the cause.
PROVEN: inverter_events_clean contains duplicate rows for the same
        event_id, despite a dedup step having already run against it.
PROVEN: those duplicate rows, summed in Gold, account for the gap
        between the reported and expected kWh total.
NOT YET PROVEN: why the dedup step let these specific 79 rows through
        when it's supposed to catch exactly this.
```

Lesson 16 reads the Glue ETL's actual dedup code next — and the answer turns out to hinge on exactly which column that `dropDuplicates` call is keyed on.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced Renata's 'August total looks too high' complaint for INST-04821 layer by layer instead of assuming a meter fault. Raw S3 data for the installation is normal -- about 8,924 readings at the expected cadence. inverter_events_clean for the same scope has 9,003 rows against only 8,924 distinct event_id values -- 79 duplicate rows in a table whose whole job is deduplication. Those duplicates, summed, account for the gap in monthly_billing_gold. Haven't read the dedup code yet, but the problem is isolated to the Clean layer, not Gold's math and not the hardware.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Billing flagged a batch of installations with kWh totals that looked almost double their normal usage. We ruled out hardware by checking the raw sensor data directly, and traced the real problem to the cleanup step of our pipeline, which is letting some duplicate readings through. We know exactly which table and which rows are affected, and we're not yet billing anyone off this number until it's fixed.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our billing team caught a batch of unusually high energy totals before any member was billed for them. We've confirmed the solar equipment itself is working fine -- this is a data pipeline issue, now isolated to one specific step, and no incorrect bill has gone out. We'll have the root cause and a fix in the next step.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing a Kinesis Retry That Double-Counted Events
lessons.summary: Reading the Glue ETL's real dedup code to find why it missed 79 duplicate readings, tracing the cause to a Kinesis/Lambda retry, fixing the dedup key, backfilling August, and adding a regression test.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved `inverter_events_clean` contains duplicate rows for `INST-04821` despite having already run through a deduplication step — and found the duplicates share the one field guaranteed unique on every raw record, `event_id`. This lesson opens the Glue ETL job's actual code from Lesson 10, finds the exact line responsible — a `dropDuplicates` call keyed on `installation_id` and `reading_timestamp` instead of `event_id` — and traces why that composite key wasn't actually unique for these 79 rows: a Kinesis/Lambda retry inside `ingest-inverter-events` wrote the same batch to S3 twice, and the retried copy's `reading_timestamp` came back serialized with a different value than the original.

By the end of this lesson, the Glue job dedupes on the true unique key, August's affected installations are backfilled in Curated and recomputed in Gold, and a new automated check exists whose entire job is making sure this exact mistake can't silently reappear.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a mail room that's supposed to throw away any letter it's already received, by checking the name on the envelope. But instead of checking the actual tracking number stamped inside every letter, the mail room only compares the sender's name and the date on the envelope. Normally that works fine — until a letter that got sent twice comes back with the date stamped very slightly differently the second time, and the mail room's check lets it through as if it were a brand new letter.

That's exactly what happened here. The cleanup step was checking "same solar panel, same reading time" instead of checking the one tag every reading actually has that's truly unique. When the system occasionally resent the same batch of readings, the resent copy's timestamp came back just slightly different, so the duplicate slipped past the check. The fix is making the cleanup step check the real unique tag instead.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The root cause is a dedup key that looks unique but isn't guaranteed to be. Reading the actual Lesson 10 ETL code:

```python
clean_df = parsed_df.dropDuplicates(["installation_id", "reading_timestamp"])
```

`installation_id` plus `reading_timestamp` is a reasonable-looking natural key — in the overwhelming majority of cases, one installation only reports one reading per timestamp. It is not, however, a *guaranteed* key, because `reading_timestamp` is a value that passes through serialization twice: once on the inverter/gateway side when the event is first produced, and again whenever `ingest-inverter-events` re-processes a batch on retry. Kinesis and Lambda together provide at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once — a transient downstream timeout during `ingest-inverter-events`'s S3 write can cause Lambda to retry a batch it had actually already written successfully, producing a second raw object in `s3://caldera-lake-raw/inverter_events/` for the same underlying `event_id`. In the specific 79 rows affecting `INST-04821`, the retried copy's `reading_timestamp` string came back with a different sub-second value than the original — enough to make `(installation_id, reading_timestamp)` look like two distinct rows to `dropDuplicates`, even though `event_id`, generated once at the source and never re-derived, was identical both times.

The diagnostic proof is direct: grouping `inverter_events_clean` by `event_id` and filtering to `count(*) > 1` returns exactly the 79 rows from Lesson 15, and for each one the two surviving rows have identical `event_id` and `installation_id` but `reading_timestamp` values that differ by a handful of milliseconds — the signature of a re-serialized retry, not a sensor sending two genuinely different readings. The fix doesn't require touching the ingestion Lambda at all; it requires deduplicating on the field that's actually guaranteed invariant across a retry, which `event_id` already is, by design, from the moment the reading is first generated.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Read the Lesson 10 dedup line with the Lesson 15 evidence in hand

```python
# glue_jobs/inverter_events_transform.py (BEFORE -- the bug, as built in Lesson 10)
def transform_raw_to_clean(raw_df):
    parsed = raw_df.withColumn("reading_timestamp", to_timestamp(col("reading_timestamp")))
    clean_df = parsed.dropDuplicates(["installation_id", "reading_timestamp"])
    return clean_df
```

`installation_id` + `reading_timestamp` looks unique and almost always is — which is exactly why this got past code review in Lesson 10. It just isn't *guaranteed* unique, and Lesson 15's 79 duplicate rows are the proof.

## Step 2 — Confirm the exact mechanism: group by the true unique key

```sql
SELECT event_id, installation_id,
       array_agg(reading_timestamp) AS timestamps,
       count(*) AS n
FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821'
GROUP BY event_id, installation_id
HAVING count(*) > 1;
-- event_id: 7f3e2b9a-...-c112   n: 2
-- timestamps: [2026-08-14 09:35:02.118, 2026-08-14 09:35:02.431]
```

Same `event_id`, same `installation_id`, `reading_timestamp` differing by 313 milliseconds — not two real readings, one `event_id` re-serialized twice across a Lambda retry.

## Step 3 — Confirm the retry in the raw layer, not just its symptom in Clean

```sql
SELECT event_id, count(*) AS raw_copies
FROM caldera_energy.raw_inverter_events
WHERE event_id = '7f3e2b9a-...-c112'
GROUP BY event_id;
-- raw_copies: 2
```

The duplicate already exists in Raw — `ingest-inverter-events` wrote this event to S3 twice. The Glue job's dedup step was Caldera's one remaining chance to catch it, and the weak key let it through.

## Step 4 — Fix the dedup key

```python
# glue_jobs/inverter_events_transform.py (AFTER -- the fix)
def transform_raw_to_clean(raw_df):
    parsed = raw_df.withColumn("reading_timestamp", to_timestamp(col("reading_timestamp")))
    clean_df = parsed.dropDuplicates(["event_id"])
    return clean_df
```

`event_id` is generated once, at the source, and never re-derived on retry — it is the one field actually guaranteed invariant across a resend, which is exactly what a dedup key needs to be.

## Step 5 — Backfill August for the affected installations

```sql
-- 1. Identify every affected installation/month before touching anything
SELECT installation_id, date_trunc('month', reading_timestamp) AS affected_month, count(*) AS dup_rows
FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
GROUP BY installation_id, reading_timestamp, event_id
HAVING count(*) > 1;
```

```bash
# 2. Re-run the fixed Glue job against the August raw partition only,
#    overwriting the affected inverter_events_clean partition
aws glue start-job-run --job-name clean-inverter-events \
  --arguments '{"--partition_month":"2026-08"}'

# 3. Recompute the Gold aggregates for the same scope via Step Functions,
#    targeting only the affected installations and month
aws stepfunctions start-execution \
  --state-machine-arn arn:aws:states:us-east-1:...:caldera-pipeline \
  --input '{"mode":"backfill","partition_month":"2026-08","installation_ids":["INST-04821", "..."]}'
```

```sql
-- 4. Confirm the backfilled total
SELECT installation_id, total_kwh FROM gold.monthly_billing_gold
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821' AND billing_month = '2026-08-01';
-- total_kwh: 931.4  (matches the trailing-twelve-month average Renata flagged against)
```

## Step 6 — Add a regression test that encodes the actual bug

```python
# tests/test_inverter_events_transform.py
def test_same_event_id_with_resend_jitter_collapses_to_one_row(spark):
    # reproduces the real August bug: same event_id, reading_timestamp
    # differs by milliseconds because of a Lambda retry re-serializing it
    raw = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("7f3e2b9a-c112", "INST-04821", "2026-08-14T09:35:02.118Z", 2.3),
        ("7f3e2b9a-c112", "INST-04821", "2026-08-14T09:35:02.431Z", 2.3),
    ], ["event_id", "installation_id", "reading_timestamp", "kwh_interval"])
    result = transform_raw_to_clean(raw)
    assert result.count() == 1
```

This test fails against the old `dropDuplicates(["installation_id", "reading_timestamp"])` and passes against the fix — which is what makes it an actual regression test for this bug, not just a generic duplicate-row check. It now runs on every pull request via Lesson 13's CI job, so this exact mistake fails a PR instead of reaching production again.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Root cause: the Glue ETL's dropDuplicates(['installation_id', 'reading_timestamp']) looked like a unique key but wasn't guaranteed to be -- a Kinesis/Lambda at-least-once retry in ingest-inverter-events occasionally wrote the same event_id to raw S3 twice, with reading_timestamp re-serialized a few hundred milliseconds apart each time, which the composite key treated as two distinct readings. Fixed by deduping on event_id, the one field actually invariant across a retry. Backfilled the affected August partition in Curated and recomputed the affected installations in Gold -- INST-04821 now matches its historical average. Added a pytest regression test reproducing the exact timestamp-jitter scenario, wired into Lesson 13's CI so this can't silently come back.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found and fixed the real cause of the inflated billing totals: an occasional network-level retry was causing a few readings to get recorded twice, and our cleanup step wasn't catching it because it was checking the wrong combination of fields. It's fixed, the affected August billing numbers have been corrected before going final, and we've added an automatic test specifically for this scenario so it can't happen again without being caught immediately.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found and corrected the root cause of the inflated energy totals: an occasional technical retry in our data pipeline was recording a small number of readings twice. No final bill went out with the inflated numbers, the affected accounts' totals are now corrected, and we've put a permanent automated safeguard in place so this specific issue can't recur without being caught the same day.

lessons.title: Connecting a BI Dashboard to the Gold Tables in Redshift
lessons.summary: Wiring Amazon QuickSight to gold.installation_performance_gold and gold.monthly_billing_gold -- and only those two tables -- so Field Ops and Billing finally have real dashboards instead of a monthly CSV export into a spreadsheet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything built so far -- Kinesis, Lambda, the raw and curated S3 layers, the Glue catalog, the two Gold tables in Redshift, the `caldera-nightly-pipeline` Step Functions state machine, and the dedup fix from Lesson 16 -- exists to produce two trustworthy numbers: how each of Caldera Energy Co-op's roughly 5,000 installations is actually performing, and what each member's monthly net-metering credit should be. None of that replaces the old manual process yet if the only way to see it is a Redshift SQL client. This video connects Amazon QuickSight directly to `gold.installation_performance_gold` and `gold.monthly_billing_gold` and builds two real dashboards on top of them: a Field Ops health dashboard for Desmond Okafor's team, and a billing dashboard for Priya Shah's Billing & Finance team.

The one rule that matters more than any individual chart: QuickSight is only ever allowed to see the two Gold tables. It never connects to `caldera-lake-raw`, never queries `caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean` in the curated layer, and never touches the Kinesis stream directly. Those layers exist to produce the Gold tables correctly -- once they have, nothing downstream should be able to reach past them and recompute its own version of "how much did this installation generate this month," which is exactly the kind of parallel, unverified number that produced Harlan Voss's spreadsheet dispute back in Lesson 1.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bakery with a messy back kitchen -- flour everywhere, half-mixed bowls, timers going off -- and a clean front counter where the finished, labeled pies are set out for customers. You'd never let a customer wander into the kitchen and grab a half-baked pie straight off the counter; they get the finished one from the display case, every time.

That's what we're building here. The Kinesis stream, the raw files, and the Glue cleanup are the messy kitchen -- necessary, but not something anyone outside the kitchen should be looking at directly. The two Gold tables are the display case: finished, checked, ready to serve. The dashboard only ever looks in the display case.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the moment a data platform either earns the trust it was built for or quietly loses it, and the mechanism is almost entirely about access boundaries, not visualization skill. Any BI tool technically *can* query `caldera-lake-curated` directly -- it's just Parquet files registered in the Glue Data Catalog, reachable through a Redshift Spectrum external schema or Athena -- and the temptation to do that "just for one chart" is exactly how a platform ends up with two slightly different answers to the same question again, the same failure mode this whole project was commissioned to retire. The fix is structural, not a policy memo: the QuickSight service role and the Redshift database user it connects as are granted `SELECT` on the `gold` schema only, nothing on `caldera_spectrum` or any raw bucket, so there is no connection a dashboard builder could configure that would let them bypass the Gold tables by accident.

The second real decision is SPICE versus direct query. QuickSight's SPICE engine imports and caches data for fast, cost-predictable dashboards instead of re-querying Redshift on every click -- the right choice here, since both Gold tables only change once per `caldera-nightly-pipeline` run, not continuously. Rather than guessing a refresh time and hoping the nightly run finished by then, the last state in that same Step Functions state machine invokes a small Lambda that calls QuickSight's `CreateIngestion` API directly, so the SPICE refresh is triggered by the pipeline actually finishing, not by a clock that might race it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Grant QuickSight exactly one schema, nothing else

```sql
-- Run once, against Redshift, as an admin
CREATE USER quicksight_reader WITH PASSWORD DISABLE;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA gold TO quicksight_reader;
GRANT SELECT ON gold.installation_performance_gold TO quicksight_reader;
GRANT SELECT ON gold.monthly_billing_gold TO quicksight_reader;
-- Deliberately no GRANT on caldera_spectrum (the external schema over
-- the curated Glue Catalog) or any raw-layer object -- quicksight_reader
-- cannot see curated or raw data even if someone later tries to point
-- a new dataset at it.
```

The matching QuickSight service IAM role gets `redshift:GetClusterCredentials` scoped to this one database user, not a cluster admin. A dashboard author inside QuickSight physically cannot browse to a raw or curated table -- the connection only ever resolves the `gold` schema.

## Step 2 -- Create two QuickSight datasets, one per Gold table

In QuickSight: **Datasets > New dataset > Amazon Redshift**, connecting through the existing Redshift-managed VPC connection, authenticating as `quicksight_reader`.

```
Dataset 1: caldera_installation_performance
  Source: gold.installation_performance_gold
  Columns: installation_id, performance_date, kwh_total,
           reading_count, fault_reading_count, panel_health_flag
  Import mode: SPICE

Dataset 2: caldera_monthly_billing
  Source: gold.monthly_billing_gold
  Columns: installation_id, billing_month, total_kwh,
           net_metering_rate_usd, net_metering_credit_amount
  Import mode: SPICE
```

## Step 3 -- Tie the SPICE refresh to the pipeline finishing, not a guessed clock time

```python
# lambda: refresh-quicksight-datasets (final state in the
# caldera-nightly-pipeline state machine, runs only after both Gold
# tables have been rebuilt)
import boto3
qs = boto3.client("quicksight")

for dataset_id in ["caldera_installation_performance", "caldera_monthly_billing"]:
    qs.create_ingestion(
        DataSetId=dataset_id,
        IngestionId=f"refresh-{dataset_id}-{context.aws_request_id}",
        AwsAccountId=ACCOUNT_ID,
    )
```

This replaces a fixed refresh schedule that could run before Step Functions has actually finished -- the dashboard refreshes the moment Gold is really current, never before.

## Step 4 -- Build the Field Ops analysis on installation_performance_gold

A table filtered to `panel_health_flag = 'FAULT'` or `'WARNING'`, a KPI card counting installations whose `reading_count` for the day is well below their normal cadence (a telemetry gap, not just a bad reading), and a trend line of `kwh_total` by region -- so Desmond's team can see a dead or degraded inverter directly, instead of waiting on a member's call.

## Step 5 -- Build the billing analysis on monthly_billing_gold, with column-level security

Finance and Member Services need to see `net_metering_credit_amount` next to the member's installation and billing month. Ops should never see billing dollar figures on the same screen as performance data. Set the billing dashboard's sharing so only the `Billing-MemberServices` QuickSight group can open `caldera_monthly_billing`; the Field Ops group only ever sees `caldera_installation_performance`.

## Step 6 -- Validate one row by hand before sharing either dashboard

```sql
SELECT installation_id, billing_month, total_kwh, net_metering_credit_amount
FROM gold.monthly_billing_gold
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-02214' AND billing_month = '2026-09-01';
```

Compare that row to the same installation's card in the published dashboard before anyone outside the project sees it. If they don't match exactly, something in the dataset's SPICE import or a QuickSight calculated field is altering the number -- find and fix that before Lesson 18's meeting, not during it.

## Step 7 -- Share each dashboard with the right group, not with everyone

```
QuickSight groups:
  Field-Ops              -> caldera_installation_performance only
  Billing-MemberServices  -> caldera_monthly_billing only
  Data-Engineering        -> both, for troubleshooting
```

Sharing both dashboards with everyone by default feels generous, but it quietly recreates the exact problem this platform was built to retire: a field technician staring at a member's dollar credit with no context for why it moved, or a billing analyst pulling up installation-health detail that isn't theirs to interpret. Scoping each dashboard to the group that actually owns the decisions it informs keeps every number attached to someone who knows what it means.

## Step 8 -- Confirm the refresh actually landed before calling this done

After the first real `caldera-nightly-pipeline` run following this setup, check **QuickSight > Datasets > caldera_monthly_billing > Refresh history** and confirm the ingestion triggered by Step 3's Lambda shows `Completed`, not `Failed` or simply missing. A SPICE dataset that silently stops refreshing looks, to Priya or Renata, exactly like a correct dashboard -- it just quietly shows last month's numbers instead of this month's, which is a harder problem to notice than an obvious error message.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Connected QuickSight to Redshift through a dedicated quicksight_reader user with SELECT granted only on the gold schema -- no path exists from the dashboard back into caldera_spectrum or raw data. Both datasets run in SPICE, refreshed by a Lambda that calls QuickSight's CreateIngestion API as the last state in the caldera-nightly-pipeline run, so the dashboard is never stale relative to the pipeline and never refreshes against a half-finished Gold rebuild.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Field Ops and Billing now each have a real dashboard instead of waiting on a SQL query from me, or in Billing's case, a manual CSV export. Both read from the same two Gold tables everyone already agreed were correct -- there's no separate path for a dashboard to quietly show a different number than the pipeline produced.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The team now has a live dashboard for installation health, and Billing and Member Services have one for monthly net-metering credits -- both built directly on the numbers the pipeline already validated, with no way for a report to drift from what the data actually says.

lessons.title: Presenting the Corrected Billing Numbers to Finance and Member Services
lessons.summary: The real meeting: walking Priya Shah's Billing team and Renata Vance's Member Services team through the now-trustworthy August billing dashboard, naming the INST-04821 dedup bug directly, and explaining why this time nobody's statement ever went out wrong.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the meeting the dashboard from Lesson 17 was actually built for: Priya Shah and Renata Vance sitting down to look at `gold.monthly_billing_gold` together, with August's billing cycle as the live example -- the same month Priya's team flagged `INST-04821` and a few dozen installations like it for showing kWh totals nearly double their trailing-twelve-month average, and the same month Lessons 15 and 16 traced that to Kinesis-retry duplicates slipping past a composite dedup key in the Glue ETL job.

The work in this video isn't technical. It's explaining, clearly and without hedging, what happened, why the original dedup key looked reasonable when it was written, what's now in place to catch it, and -- the part that actually matters to Renata's team -- the fact that because this was caught before August's billing run finalized, no member ever received a statement with the inflated number on it. That's the real difference this project was built to deliver, and it's worth saying out loud next to Harlan Voss's spreadsheet-era dispute from Lesson 1, where the wrong number did go out and he had to call in to find out why.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a smoke detector that goes off while something is just starting to smell a little hot -- before anything actually catches fire. That's a very different, much better outcome than finding out about a fire because the kitchen is already smoking when someone walks in. Both situations involve something going wrong, but catching it early means nobody ever got hurt and nothing ever had to be repaired after the fact.

That's this meeting. A glitch in counting almost inflated some members' credit for one month. But because the team was watching closely, it got caught and fixed before any bill went out -- nobody ever saw a wrong number on their statement. The job now is to calmly explain exactly what almost happened, and why nobody needs to worry about this month's bill.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The framing of this meeting matters because the direction and the timing of the error both work in Caldera's favor here, and it would be a mistake to undersell that by treating this as just another bug-fix status update. `INST-04821`'s August total was computed as 1,842.6 kWh against a trailing-twelve-month average of roughly 930 -- close to double -- which at the board-approved $0.1125/kWh net-metering rate would have meant a credit of about $207.29 instead of the correct $104.78. That's a real, material error, but it was caught by Priya's team comparing the number against installation history *before* `monthly_billing_gold` was finalized and exported for the August billing run, which means the honest, accurate statement to make in this room is: nobody's bill went out wrong this cycle.

The technical explanation has to be specific enough to survive scrutiny without becoming a liability-admission exercise: during an ordinary Kinesis/Lambda at-least-once retry inside `ingest-inverter-events`, the same telemetry event was written to `caldera-lake-raw` twice, with its `reading_timestamp` re-serialized a few hundred milliseconds apart each time. The Glue ETL's original dedup step, keyed on `installation_id` and `reading_timestamp`, looked defensible when it was written in Lesson 10 -- two genuine readings landing in the exact same timestamp was never the scenario it was designed to catch -- but a retry's jitter fell inside that same key and slipped through undetected for 79 rows on this one installation alone. Deduplicating on the inverter's own `event_id` instead closes that specific gap, and a pytest regression test reproducing the exact timestamp-jitter scenario now runs on every pull request through Lesson 13's CI, so this precise mistake can't be reintroduced without failing a build. The harder, more honest point to make in the room -- saved for the next lesson's wrap-up, but worth naming here too -- is that this was caught by a human comparing a number against history, not by any of Lesson 14's CloudWatch alarms, which watch for infrastructure failures and lag, not for a Gold-layer total that's quietly wrong while every upstream service reports healthy.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Prepare the exact numbers before walking in

```
AUGUST BILLING CYCLE -- INST-04821, THE TRACED EXAMPLE

Trailing twelve-month average:              ~930 kWh / month
Computed total BEFORE the fix (the bug):     1,842.6 kWh
  -> credit at $0.1125/kWh:                  $207.29
Corrected total AFTER the Lesson 16 backfill: 931.4 kWh
  -> credit at $0.1125/kWh:                  $104.78
Root cause:                                   79 duplicate event_id
                                               rows in
                                               inverter_events_clean,
                                               caused by a Kinesis/
                                               Lambda retry the old
                                               dedup key didn't catch
Scope:                                         INST-04821 plus a few
                                               dozen other installations
                                               in the same August batch,
                                               all identified and
                                               backfilled before the
                                               billing run finalized
Member statements affected:                   ZERO -- caught before
                                               export, unlike Harlan
                                               Voss's spreadsheet-era
                                               dispute in Lesson 1
```

Having the exact traced figures ready, not an estimate given live, is what keeps this a status update instead of a negotiation.

## Step 2 -- Open with the one fact that matters most, plainly

```
"The August billing numbers you're looking at now are correct, and I
want to lead with this: no member received a statement with a wrong
number on it this cycle. We caught an issue before the billing run
finalized, fixed it, and I want to walk through exactly what it was
and why I'm confident saying that."
```

## Step 3 -- Explain the mechanism without jargon, using the one real installation

```sql
-- Projected live: INST-04821's event count before and after the fix
SELECT installation_id, COUNT(*) AS raw_copies,
       COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS true_unique_events
FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
WHERE installation_id = 'INST-04821'
  AND reading_timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-08-01' AND TIMESTAMP '2026-08-31 23:59:59';
-- raw_copies (before fix): 9,003   true_unique_events: 8,924
```

```
"Our cleanup step checked for duplicate readings by looking at the
installation and the exact minute a reading came in -- that made
sense, because these inverters only report every few minutes, so two
genuine readings in the same instant was never expected. During a
network-level retry in August, the same reading got resent and came
back with its timestamp recorded a few hundred milliseconds
differently, which slipped past that check 79 times for this one
installation. We've switched to checking the unique ID the inverter
itself stamps on every reading -- that catches this exact situation --
and we've added an automatic test that runs on every single change to
this code from here forward."
```

## Step 4 -- Name plainly what caught it, and what didn't

```
YOU: "I want to be specific about how this was caught, because it
      matters for what we do next: it wasn't one of our automated
      alarms. Priya's team noticed INST-04821's total looked almost
      double its usual history and flagged it before the billing run
      went out. Our current monitoring watches for the pipeline
      failing or falling behind -- it doesn't yet watch for a number
      that's quietly wrong while everything upstream reports healthy.
      That's a real gap, and it's worth talking about as we close
      out this series."
PRIYA: "I'd rather know that now than assume the dashboard would have
        caught it for us."
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm there is nothing left for Member Services to do this cycle

```
RENATA: "So nobody calls in about this one, the way Harlan did?"
YOU:    "Right -- August's statements go out with the corrected
         numbers, on schedule. There's no notice to send, because
         nothing a member would have seen was ever wrong. If you'd
         like, I can give your team a one-line internal note for your
         own records, in case this ever comes up."
RENATA: "Let's keep that internal. No reason to raise something that
         never reached a member."
```

That's a real, defensible call for Member Services to make, and it's theirs to make -- not a decision the engineer presenting the fix should make for them.

## Step 6 -- Log the incident and close with the forward-looking commitment

Record the root cause, the 79-row count, the corrected totals, and Renata's decision not to notify members in a dated internal memo -- this is the artifact Member Services points to if the question ever comes up later. Close the meeting by confirming the Lesson 17 dashboard and the Lesson 13/14 tests and alarms are what Billing and Member Services rely on going forward, not a return to the manual CSV-and-spreadsheet process from before this project started.

Named plainly that this was caught by Priya's team comparing a number against history, not by any of the CloudWatch alarms -- an honest gap to carry into the closing lesson.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Got Billing and Member Services aligned on the corrected August numbers and confirmed the key fact that makes this project a real win: no member statement went out wrong this cycle. Renata made the call that no member notification is needed, since nothing a member would have seen was ever incorrect -- that's documented for the record.
workplaceExplanation.executive: A billing error that would have overcredited members by roughly double was caught and corrected before a single statement went out -- a direct contrast to the spreadsheet-era dispute that got this project funded in the first place. Nobody needs to be contacted, and we've documented exactly what happened and what's now in place to catch it even earlier next time.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Docs: Data Dictionary, Lineage, and an On-Call Runbook
lessons.summary: Writing a plain-English data dictionary entry for Monthly Billing Credit, a prose lineage description from inverter to dashboard, and an on-call runbook that tells whoever's paged exactly where to look first -- and admits where the real gap still is.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The pipeline works, the dashboard is live, and the August near-miss from Lessons 15, 16, and 18 is documented and closed -- but none of that survives you leaving the project unless it's written down somewhere a future on-call engineer, or Priya's successor, can actually find and use. This video writes the three documents that make this platform maintainable by someone who wasn't in any of the previous eighteen meetings: a data dictionary entry for "Monthly Billing Credit" that states plainly what it means and what it deliberately excludes, a prose description of the full data lineage from inverter to dashboard, and an on-call runbook entry that turns "the billing number looks wrong" or "the dashboard looks stale" from a panic into an ordered checklist.

These three documents answer three different questions for three different readers. The dictionary answers a Billing analyst's "what exactly am I looking at." The lineage answers a new engineer's "where does this number actually come from." The runbook answers the 2 a.m. page's "what do I check first, in what order" -- and, honestly, names the one failure mode none of those checks would have caught.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you build a really good treehouse, and then you move away. If you don't leave notes, whoever moves in next has to figure out which board holds up the roof by trial and error -- possibly by falling through it. So you leave three notes: one explaining what each room is for, one showing how water gets from the roof to the rain barrel step by step, and one taped right by the door saying "if it starts creaking, check these three things first, in this order." That's what this video writes, for a data pipeline instead of a treehouse.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A platform's documentation quality is usually invisible right up until the moment someone other than its builder has to act on it under time pressure, which is exactly the condition an on-call page creates. The data dictionary entry has to do something most dictionary entries skip: state the exclusion list, not just the definition, because "what does this number NOT include" is almost always where a stakeholder's assumption and the actual calculation quietly diverge -- Monthly Billing Credit excludes readings whose panel-health status was flagged degraded or invalid at the time they were reported (per the Lesson 2 acceptance criteria), and it excludes any event_id already counted once, which is the exact mechanism the August incident exposed.

The lineage description's job is narrower but just as load-bearing: it has to name every real hop by its real name -- the `caldera-inverter-telemetry` stream, the `ingest-inverter-events` Lambda, the `caldera-lake-raw` and `caldera-lake-curated` buckets, the `caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean` Glue Catalog table, the `caldera_spectrum` Redshift Spectrum external schema, and the two Gold tables -- so a reader can trace a wrong number back to a specific stage without guessing. The runbook's job is to be ordered by actual diagnostic cost, cheapest signal first, and to end with the one honest caveat this whole series earned the hard way in Lesson 18: none of the first four checks would have caught the August dedup issue, because it wasn't an infrastructure failure. A runbook that implies otherwise would send the next on-call engineer looking in the wrong place.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the Monthly Billing Credit dictionary entry, exclusions included

```
METRIC: Monthly Billing Credit
DEFINITION: The dollar credit applied to a member's account for one
            billing month -- gold.monthly_billing_gold.net_metering_
            credit_amount, computed as that installation's total_kwh
            for the month multiplied by net_metering_rate_usd (the
            board-approved rate, currently $0.1125/kWh).
WHAT THIS EXCLUDES:
  - Readings flagged degraded or invalid at the panel-health level at
    the time they were reported are never counted toward total_kwh,
    per the Lesson 2 acceptance criteria.
  - Any event_id already counted once is excluded from every later
    count, by design -- this is the exact mechanism that nearly over-
    credited INST-04821 and a few dozen other installations in
    August before Lesson 16's fix.
  - A telemetry reading that arrives after the billing month has
    already been loaded into monthly_billing_gold is not retro-
    actively added -- it is picked up in the following month's run.
WHERE IT LIVES: gold.monthly_billing_gold, column
    net_metering_credit_amount.
LAST CHANGED: the Glue ETL's dedup key changed from
    (installation_id, reading_timestamp) to event_id after the August
    incident; see the pytest regression test added to
    caldera-clean-inverter-events at the same time.
OWNER: Data Engineering, with Priya Shah's Billing & Finance team as
    required reviewer for any change to the net-metering rate itself.
```

## Step 2 -- Write the lineage as prose, naming every real resource

```
Each of Caldera's roughly 5,000 smart inverters publishes a telemetry
event every few minutes directly to the caldera-inverter-telemetry
Kinesis stream. The ingest-inverter-events Lambda function reads from
that stream and writes each event, largely as received, into the
caldera-lake-raw S3 bucket. The caldera-clean-inverter-events Glue ETL
job then cleans the data, deduplicates on true event_id, and writes
the result into caldera-lake-curated, where it's registered in the
Glue Data Catalog as caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean. Redshift
reads that curated table through a Spectrum external schema,
caldera_spectrum, and loads two Gold tables:
gold.installation_performance_gold, one row per installation per day,
and gold.monthly_billing_gold, one row per installation per billing
month -- the only two tables anything outside the pipeline is allowed
to read from. Amazon QuickSight connects to those two Gold tables, and
only those two, to produce the Field Ops and Billing dashboards. Every
stage from the Kinesis stream through the final Redshift load is
orchestrated end to end by the caldera-nightly-pipeline Step Functions
state machine, which also triggers the QuickSight SPICE refresh once
Gold is current.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the on-call runbook entry, cheapest check first, honest caveat last

```
RUNBOOK: Pipeline looks stale, or a billing number looks wrong

1. CHECK KINESIS ITERATOR AGE first (cheapest, fastest signal).
   CloudWatch metric: GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds on
   caldera-inverter-telemetry (alarm:
   caldera-inverter-telemetry-iterator-age, threshold 60,000ms). A
   rising iterator age means ingest-inverter-events is falling behind
   real-time -- the Lambda is the likely bottleneck, not anything
   downstream.

2. CHECK LAMBDA ERRORS on ingest-inverter-events.
   CloudWatch metric: Errors (alarm:
   caldera-ingest-inverter-events-errors). A spike here, correlated
   with the iterator-age rise in Step 1, usually means a downstream
   dependency is rejecting writes, not a code regression.

3. CHECK THE GLUE JOB RUN HISTORY for caldera-clean-inverter-events
   and its crawler. AWS Glue console > Jobs > Run history. A failed
   or still-running job explains why caldera-lake-curated, and
   everything after it, hasn't updated.

4. CHECK STEP FUNCTIONS EXECUTION HISTORY for caldera-nightly-pipeline
   (alarm: caldera-pipeline-state-machine-failures, notifies via the
   caldera-pipeline-alerts SNS topic). Look for a failed state around
   the time the issue was first noticed -- this tells you exactly
   which stage stopped the whole chain, faster than checking each
   service individually.

5. IF THE NUMBER LOOKS WRONG specifically -- not stale, just off --
   run the dedup regression query directly against the affected
   billing month:
     SELECT installation_id, COUNT(*) AS raw,
       COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS deduped
     FROM caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
     WHERE reading_timestamp >= '<month_start>'
       AND reading_timestamp < '<next_month_start>'
     GROUP BY installation_id HAVING COUNT(*) <> COUNT(DISTINCT event_id);
   A non-empty result means a duplicate-event pattern has resurfaced.

   HONEST CAVEAT: Steps 1 through 4 watch for the pipeline failing or
   falling behind. None of them would have caught August's incident,
   because every service reported healthy the whole time -- the
   problem was a quietly wrong number, not a failure. Step 5's query,
   or a human noticing a total looks unusual against history, is
   currently the only way this specific failure mode gets caught.
```

## Step 4 -- Store all three where the next person will actually find them

Commit the dictionary entry and lineage description into the project's internal wiki under "Caldera Billing Platform," not a personal notes file, and pin the runbook entry directly in the on-call tool's knowledge base so it surfaces automatically when a relevant CloudWatch alarm fires.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wrote the Monthly Billing Credit dictionary entry with its exclusions spelled out, a prose lineage description naming every real resource from the Kinesis stream through the Gold tables to QuickSight, and an on-call runbook ordered from cheapest check (Kinesis iterator age) to most thorough (a direct dedup regression query) -- with an explicit note that none of the infrastructure alarms would have caught August's incident on their own. All three are in the team wiki and the on-call knowledge base, not a personal file.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've documented what the billing number actually means, where it comes from end to end, and exactly what to check first if something looks wrong -- including an honest note about which kind of problem this runbook can't yet catch by itself. That protects this project from becoming dependent on one person's memory or judgment.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The platform is now documented well enough that someone other than the person who built it can maintain it -- what the billing number means, where it comes from, and what to check first if anything looks off. We've also been upfront about the one category of problem this documentation can't fully solve on its own, which is exactly the kind of honesty that keeps this platform trustworthy.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the whole Caldera Energy Co-op build -- what's genuinely automated and trustworthy now, and what still depends on a human noticing something and acting on it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Caldera Energy Co-op went from a manual CSV-and-spreadsheet process that had already produced one real, disputed billing number -- Harlan Voss's credit swinging from $84.00 to $211.60 because a week of data got pasted into the monthly workbook twice -- to a genuine, running AWS data platform: roughly 5,000 solar installations streaming telemetry through Kinesis and Lambda into a real data lake, cataloged and cleaned by Glue, aggregated into two Gold tables in Redshift, orchestrated end to end by the `caldera-nightly-pipeline` Step Functions state machine, tested by CI, watched by CloudWatch and SNS, and surfaced in a live QuickSight dashboard that Field Ops and Billing actually use. A real near-miss -- Kinesis-retry duplicates slipping past a composite dedup key and nearly doubling August's billing total for `INST-04821` and a few dozen installations like it -- was found, root-caused, fixed, and backfilled before a single statement went out. That part is real and it's done.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what still depends on a human, what's reduced rather than eliminated, and what would need real additional work before anyone should call this platform "finished."
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you spent months building a really solid new bridge to replace a rickety wooden one everyone was scared to cross. The new bridge is genuinely strong -- it's inspected, it has guardrails, it has warning lights if something's wrong. But a good engineer doesn't just say "it's perfect, never think about it again" -- they say "this is solid, but the warning lights still need a person to actually look at them and decide what to do, and some kinds of wear and tear still need someone to walk across and check by hand, because the lights don't catch everything." That honesty is what makes the bridge actually safe to keep using. This video is that same honest walkthrough, for the data platform instead of a bridge.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it restates the real, finished architecture plainly enough for someone who missed the first nineteen videos to understand what's actually running, and it names the real remaining gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the August incident -- not "there's room for improvement," but three named, concrete limitations. First, the CloudWatch alarms and SNS notifications from Lesson 14 still require a human to triage and act on every page; nothing in this platform auto-remediates a failed Glue job or a Lambda error spike, and an alarm that fires into a channel nobody is watching is functionally the same as no alarm at all. Second, the true-event_id dedup fix meaningfully reduces the double-counting risk but does not architecturally eliminate it -- it closes the specific gap August's incident exposed, but `ingest-inverter-events` still operates under Kinesis's at-least-once delivery semantics, so a different retry pattern in a different part of the pipeline could in principle produce a related issue, which is exactly why the pytest regression test exists rather than treating the fix as a permanent guarantee. Third, and this is the one Lesson 18 and 19 both surfaced directly: there is no automated data-quality monitor that would have caught August's incident on its own -- it was caught because Priya's team compared a total against trailing history, not because any CloudWatch alarm fired, and if a bad number ever did reach a final, posted statement the way Harlan Voss's did in the spreadsheet era, correcting it after the fact would still be the same kind of manual, case-by-case judgment call Renata made in Lesson 18, not an automated workflow.

Naming these plainly isn't an admission of failure -- overselling a system's completeness to Priya, Renata, or Caldera's board is itself the same category of trust problem the original spreadsheet-era dispute already caused once. The honest version of "done" is "this solved the specific, real problem it was scoped to solve, these are its real remaining edges, and here's what a future phase would need to address them."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
SOURCE:        ~5,000 smart inverters, one telemetry event every few minutes
STREAM:        caldera-inverter-telemetry (Kinesis)
INGEST:        ingest-inverter-events (Lambda)
RAW LANDING:   caldera-lake-raw (S3)
CATALOG/ETL:   caldera-clean-inverter-events (Glue crawler + ETL) --
               dedup on true event_id
CURATED:       caldera-lake-curated (S3), cataloged as
               caldera_energy.inverter_events_clean
GOLD (Redshift, via caldera_spectrum external schema):
               gold.installation_performance_gold,
               gold.monthly_billing_gold (at $0.1125/kWh)
ORCHESTRATED BY: caldera-nightly-pipeline (Step Functions), including
               the QuickSight SPICE refresh trigger
TESTED BY:     CI running on every Glue ETL and Terraform change
               (Lesson 13), including the pytest regression test for
               the August dedup bug
WATCHED BY:    CloudWatch alarms (Lambda errors, Kinesis iterator age,
               Step Functions failures) + the caldera-pipeline-alerts
               SNS topic (Lesson 14)
SURFACED IN:   Amazon QuickSight, two dashboards (Field Ops, Billing),
               reading ONLY from the Gold tables (Lesson 17)
```

Every box in that chain was built, tested, and is in real use today by Field Ops, Billing, and Member Services -- that's the genuine, defensible claim this series gets to make.

## Step 2 -- Name what's still manual, specifically

```
GAP 1: Alarms still require a human to triage and act.
  CloudWatch and SNS will page someone when iterator age spikes, a
  Lambda errors out, or a Step Functions execution fails -- but
  nothing in this platform auto-remediates. An alarm firing into a
  channel nobody is watching produces the same outcome as no alarm at
  all. The runbook from Lesson 19 makes the human response fast; it
  doesn't remove the need for one.

GAP 2: The duplicate-event risk is reduced, not architecturally
  eliminated.
  Deduplicating on true event_id closes the specific gap August's
  incident exposed. It does not mean every write in this pipeline is
  immune to Kinesis's at-least-once delivery behavior -- a different
  retry pattern somewhere else in the chain could in principle
  produce a related issue. That's exactly why the regression test
  runs on every CI build rather than treating the August fix as a
  permanent guarantee.

GAP 3: No automated check would have caught August's incident on its
  own.
  It was caught because Priya's team compared a total against
  trailing history, not because a CloudWatch alarm fired -- every
  upstream service reported healthy the entire time. And if a bad
  number ever did reach a final, posted member statement the way
  Harlan Voss's did before this project started, correcting it is
  still the same manual, case-by-case decision Renata made in Lesson
  18, not an automated workflow.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
"This project replaced a manual, dispute-prone CSV-and-spreadsheet
process with a real, automated AWS data platform that roughly 5,000
installations now report through, and it caught and fixed a genuine
billing near-miss before it ever reached a member. It did not
eliminate the need for a human to respond to monitoring alerts, did
not make every write in the pipeline provably immune to retries, and
did not add an automated check for the specific class of problem that
almost doubled August's numbers -- that was caught by a person
comparing a total against history. Those are real, named limits for a
future phase, not oversights we're pretending don't exist."
```

## Step 4 -- Leave a short, prioritized list for a possible phase two

```
1. A documented on-call rotation and escalation policy for the
   CloudWatch/SNS alarms, so Gap 1 has a committed owner at every
   hour, not just during business hours.
2. A scheduled data-quality check -- comparing each installation's
   monthly total against its own trailing history automatically,
   the same comparison Priya's team made by hand -- so Gap 3 doesn't
   keep depending on a human happening to notice.
3. A broader idempotency audit of every write path into
   caldera-lake-raw, not just the composite-key fix -- closes Gap 2
   at the architectural level instead of the incident level.
```

That's the real, unglamorous ending: not every problem solved, but every remaining one named, owned, and ready to hand to whoever maintains this platform next.
